label: What a package does
lesson:
# What a package does

A package is the structure between a bare die and a printed circuit board. It carries signals and power from the die's fine on-chip pitch out to the board's coarse pitch, removes the die's heat, protects the die mechanically and chemically, and lets the die be tested and handled. For a tool designer the package is not an afterthought: its wiring, power network, heat path and stress state become constraints that propagate back into floorplanning, I/O planning, timing and reliability signoff.

## Four jobs of a package

A package does four things at once. Electrically, it fans out hundreds to tens of thousands of die pads to board-level balls and supplies power with low impedance. Thermally, it provides the path from the transistors to a heat sink or board, usually the dominant resistance between junction and ambient. Mechanically, it holds a brittle die whose coefficient of thermal expansion (about 2.6 ppm/K for silicon) differs from the board's (roughly 14 to 18 ppm/K for FR-4), so every power cycle strains the joints in between. Environmentally, mold compound, underfill and lids seal the die against moisture and handling. A change aimed at one job almost always moves another: a thinner substrate improves signal paths but warps more, and a lid that spreads heat adds a stiff interface that changes stress.

## The interconnect hierarchy

Interconnect pitch grows by orders of magnitude from transistor to board. On-chip wires sit at tens of nanometres; top-metal pads and bumps sit at tens to about 150 micrometres; package substrate traces at roughly 10 to 25 micrometres line and space on organic build-up layers; board balls at 0.4 to 1.27 millimetres. Each level exists because the next one cannot be made at the finer pitch at acceptable cost. The package's job is to bridge the gap with as few levels and as little parasitic resistance, inductance and capacitance as possible. Advanced packaging (fan-out, interposers, hybrid bonding) inserts finer levels so that die-to-die wiring never has to descend to board pitch, which is where most of the bandwidth and energy gains come from.

## What the package feeds back into design

Package decisions become design inputs. The bump map fixes where power and each I/O can enter the die, so the floorplan and power grid must match it. Package trace and bond-wire parasitics enter signal-integrity and timing models of I/O paths. The junction-to-ambient thermal resistance sets the power budget, and with it the voltage and frequency targets. Warpage and joint strain set limits on die size and on the substrate's construction. A late package change therefore ripples into place and route, power analysis and signoff. This is why modern flows co-design die, package and board in one database instead of handing off a pin list at the end, and why EDA vendors sell package-aware floorplanning and extraction.

## Going deeper

Tummala, "Fundamentals of Microsystems Packaging" (2001); Lau, "Semiconductor Advanced Packaging" (2021); the IEEE Heterogeneous Integration Roadmap chapters on packaging.

A team thins a package substrate to shorten its vias for signal integrity. Which package job is most likely to suffer as a side effect?

A) Electrical: thinner vias always add inductance

B) Environmental: thin substrates absorb no moisture

D) Mechanical: the thinner, less stiff substrate warps more under CTE mismatch
problems.a: Mechanical: the thinner, less stiff substrate warps more under CTE mismatch
problems.e: Stiffness falls steeply with thickness, so the same CTE mismatch bends a thin substrate more. Package jobs are coupled, and a change aimed at one moves another.

problems.a: The thermal path loses one interface layer, but the die is less protected mechanically

D) Holding the standard-cell rows for placement

C) Capacitance: bumps have none

D) Resistance: bond wires are superconducting
problems.a: Inductance: a nanohenry or more for a wire against tens of picohenries for a bump

problems.e: Advanced packaging inserts finer levels so that dense die-to-die wiring stays fine-pitch.

D) The number of timing corners
problems.a: The allowed power, and with it the voltage and frequency the chip can run at
problems.e: Allowed power is the junction-to-ambient temperature budget divided by the thermal resistance, and that budget shrinks with ambient.

label: Wire bonding
lesson:
# Wire bonding

Wire bonding connects die pads to package leads with thin gold, copper or aluminium wires, bonded by heat, force and ultrasonic energy. It is the oldest and still the cheapest chip-to-package interconnect, used on most low pin-count parts. Its limits explain the move to flip chip: pads must sit on the die perimeter, so I/O count grows only linearly with die size, and each wire adds roughly a nanohenry of inductance per millimetre to every power and signal path.

## Perimeter-limited pad count

Wire-bond pads sit along the die edge, so the pad count is set by perimeter and pad pitch, not by area. A square die of side $S$ with one row of pads at pitch $p$ holds about $\lfloor S/p \rfloor$ pads per side and $4\lfloor S/p \rfloor$ in total. A 5 mm die at 60 um pitch holds $\lfloor 5000/60 \rfloor = 83$ per side, 332 in all. Two staggered rows can roughly double this, but the wires then cross at two loop heights and the bonder needs more clearance. Doubling the die side only doubles the pads while the logic grows fourfold, so large dies become pad-limited: the die must grow to fit its I/O, and silicon area is wasted. That scaling argument is the main reason high pin-count parts use area-array flip chip.

## Bond wire resistance

A bond wire is a cylinder of length $L$ and diameter $d$, so its resistance is $R = \rho L / (\pi d^2/4)$. Gold has $\rho \approx 2.44$ micro-ohm cm and copper about 1.7. A 2 mm gold wire of 25 um diameter has area $\pi (25 \times 10^{-6})^2/4 = 4.91 \times 10^{-10}$ m^2, so $R = 2.44 \times 10^{-8} \times 2 \times 10^{-3} / 4.91 \times 10^{-10} = 0.099$ ohm, about 99 milliohm. That matters for power: a 1 A supply through one such wire drops about 0.1 V. Packages therefore use many parallel power and ground wires, and copper wire is popular partly for its lower resistivity, at the cost of a harder bonding process.

## Inductance and ground bounce

The bigger electrical problem is inductance. A bond wire has a self-inductance of roughly 1 nH per millimetre, and a current change $\Delta I$ over time $t_r$ through inductance $L$ induces $V = L\,\Delta I/t_r$. If 16 outputs switch together and draw 0.4 A of extra ground current in 1 ns through a 3 nH ground wire, the ground bounces by $3 \times 0.4 / 1 = 1.2$ V, enough to corrupt logic levels. Putting $N$ ground wires in parallel divides the inductance by about $N$ when mutual coupling is ignored, so eight wires cut the bounce to 0.15 V. Real wires couple, so the improvement is smaller, which is why simultaneous switching noise is checked with extracted package models rather than with this estimate alone.

## Going deeper

Harman, "Wire Bonding in Microelectronics" (3rd ed., 2010); Bogatin, "Signal and Power Integrity, Simplified" (3rd ed., 2018), chapters on inductance.

label: Flip chip and BGA packages
prereqs: The product and sum rules for counting
lesson:
# Flip chip and BGA packages

In flip chip the die is turned face down and joined to the package by solder bumps spread over its whole area. The package then reaches the board through a ball grid array (BGA): an area array of solder balls on its underside. Both are area arrays, so I/O count grows with area rather than perimeter, and the short bumps have far less inductance than bond wires. Bump and ball counts are the first numbers a package planner computes.

## Area-array bump count

Flip-chip bumps sit on a regular grid at pitch $p$, often 130 to 200 um for solder bumps and copper pillars on mainstream parts. If the first bump is placed $p/2$ from each edge, a die of width $W$ and height $H$ holds $\lfloor W/p \rfloor \times \lfloor H/p \rfloor$ bumps. A 10 mm by 8 mm die at 150 um pitch holds $\lfloor 10000/150 \rfloor \times \lfloor 8000/150 \rfloor = 66 \times 53 = 3498$ bumps. Not all are signals: typically more than half carry power and ground, spread across the die so the on-chip power grid is fed from directly above every region. That spread is the electrical reason for an area array, beyond the raw count.

## Area array against perimeter

Take a square die whose side holds $n$ sites at a given pitch. An area array uses all $n^2$ sites, while a perimeter ring at the same pitch uses only the outer ring, $4(n-1)$ sites. For $n = 50$ that is 2500 against 196, a ratio of about 12.8, and the ratio grows linearly with $n$. Flip chip also shortens the electrical path: a bump is tens of micrometres tall with tens of picohenries of inductance, against a nanohenry or more for a bond wire. The costs are a more expensive substrate that must escape-route the dense array, underfill to protect the bumps from CTE strain, and a die whose back side, not its face, now carries the heat path.

## BGA ball maps

A BGA package of side $L$ with ball pitch $p$ has an $\lfloor L/p \rfloor$ by $\lfloor L/p \rfloor$ grid; common pitches are 1.0, 0.8, 0.65 and 0.5 mm. Many packages depopulate a central $k \times k$ block, for example to leave room under the die for thermal vias or to ease board routing, so the ball count is $\lfloor L/p \rfloor^2 - k^2$. A 35 mm package at 1.0 mm pitch with a 9 by 9 hole has $35^2 - 81 = 1144$ balls. The ball map is a co-design object: the package designer wants power balls under the die, the board designer wants signal balls on the outer rows where they escape without vias, and the ball pitch sets which board via and trace technology is needed.

## Going deeper

Lau, "Flip Chip Technologies" (1996); JEDEC publication 95 for BGA outlines; Tummala, "Fundamentals of Microsystems Packaging", chapter on flip chip.

label: Package substrates: organic and glass
lesson:
# Package substrates: organic and glass

A package substrate is the small wiring board under the die. Most are organic: a glass-fibre core with build-up dielectric layers and copper traces, made by semi-additive plating. Glass-core substrates are an emerging alternative, offering flatter panels, finer lines and a coefficient of thermal expansion that can be tuned closer to silicon. The substrate's line and space, layer count and CTE decide how many signals escape the die and how much the assembly warps.

## Wiring capacity per layer

Substrate wiring is specified by line width $w$ and space $s$. One layer carries $\lfloor 1000/(w+s) \rfloor$ traces per millimetre of edge, with $w$ and $s$ in micrometres. Organic build-up layers on mainstream substrates run around 15/15 to 8/8 um line and space; leading-edge organic and glass substrates aim lower. Across a 10 mm die edge on four signal layers at 10/10 um, capacity is $10 \times 4 \times \lfloor 1000/20 \rfloor = 2000$ traces. Wiring capacity, not bump count, is often the bottleneck: if a die needs more signals out of one edge than the substrate can carry, the designer must add layers, tighten the line and space, or move to an interposer.

## Layers needed for a signal count

Invert the capacity formula to size the stackup. If $S$ signals must cross an edge of length $E$ mm at pitch $w+s$, the number of signal layers is $\lceil S / (E \lfloor 1000/(w+s) \rfloor) \rceil$. For 3000 signals across 12 mm at 12/12 um, one layer carries $12 \times 41 = 492$, so seven layers are needed. Every build-up layer adds cost and a yield loss, and layers come in pairs on both sides of the core to keep the substrate balanced against warpage. Halving line and space roughly halves the layer count, which is the economic case for finer-line substrates and for glass, whose smooth flat surface supports finer lithography than a woven-glass organic core.

## CTE and dimensional stability

Substrate materials expand with temperature. A point at distance $D$ from the neutral point moves by $\alpha D \Delta T$, so a substrate and a die move apart by $|\alpha_{sub} - \alpha_{Si}| D \Delta T$. With an organic core at 15 ppm/K, silicon at 2.6 ppm/K, $D = 15$ mm and a 100 K swing, the mismatch is $12.4 \times 10^{-6} \times 15000 \times 100 = 18.6$ um, a large fraction of a 40 um microbump pitch. Underfill and compliant joints absorb it on flip chip, but fine-pitch die-to-die joints cannot. Glass cores can be formulated with CTE in the low single digits, much closer to silicon, and are stiffer and flatter. Their open problems are brittleness, through-glass via formation and handling of large thin panels.

## Going deeper

Tummala, "Fundamentals of Microsystems Packaging", chapter on package substrates; the IEEE Heterogeneous Integration Roadmap chapter on substrates.

label: BGA escape routing
lesson:
# BGA escape routing

Escape routing is the problem of bringing every signal out from inside a dense ball or bump array to the array's edge, so it can be routed onward. Inner balls can only leave through the channels between outer balls, so the channel capacity sets how many rows escape on each layer. This one inequality drives layer counts in package substrates and printed circuit boards alike, and it is a classic constrained routing problem for package routers.

## Traces through one channel

Between two adjacent pads of diameter $d$ at pitch $p$ the free gap is $p - d$. Placing $n$ traces of width $w$ in it needs $n$ widths and $n+1$ spaces $s$ (one to each pad and between traces), so $n w + (n+1) s \le p - d$, which gives $n = \lfloor (p - d - s)/(w + s) \rfloor$. For a 1000 um pitch with 500 um pads and 75/75 um line and space, $n = \lfloor (1000 - 500 - 75)/150 \rfloor = 2$ traces per channel. Shrinking the pad or the line and space adds channel capacity; shrinking the pitch removes it fast, which is why fine-pitch BGAs need fine-line boards with via-in-pad or microvias.

## Rows per layer and layer count

The outer row of balls escapes directly. Each channel between outer-row balls carries $n$ traces, and on each side of the array there is about one channel per ball in a row, so $n$ further rows can escape through the channels. One layer therefore escapes $n + 1$ rows. An array with $R$ rows from edge to centre needs $\lceil R/(n+1) \rceil$ routing layers, ignoring power and ground balls that drop straight down through vias. With two traces per channel and 15 rows to escape, five layers are needed. This simple count is the first estimate a planner makes before running a router, and it explains why depopulating rows or assigning inner balls to power reduces the board layer count.

## Balls escaped on the first layer

For an $N \times N$ full array, the first layer escapes the outer $k = n+1$ rings. The balls inside them number $(N - 2k)^2$ when $N > 2k$, so the escaped count is $N^2 - (N - 2k)^2$. For $N = 30$ and $k = 3$ that is $900 - 576 = 324$ balls on the first layer. The second layer, reached through vias, escapes the next $k$ rings, and so on. The rings shrink toward the centre, so later layers carry fewer balls each; a planner exploits this by putting power and ground at the centre where they need vias anyway, keeping signal rings on few layers. Package routers solve escape as a flow problem that respects these channel capacities before detailed routing.

## Going deeper

Yan and Wong, "Recent research development in PCB layout", ICCAD (2010); Fang, Lee and Chang, "A network-flow-based RDL routing algorithm for flip-chip design", IEEE TCAD (2007).

label: Wafer-level and fan-out packaging
lesson:
# Wafer-level and fan-out packaging

Wafer-level packaging builds the package on the wafer itself, before or instead of dicing into a separate substrate. In fan-in WLP the balls sit under the die, so the package is the size of the die. In fan-out WLP the dies are embedded in mold compound to form a larger reconstituted wafer or panel, and redistribution layers carry the I/O out beyond the die edge. The choice between them is a count of balls against area.

## Fan-in capacity

A fan-in WLP places solder balls directly on the die at a pitch such as 0.4 or 0.35 mm, routed from the pads by a redistribution layer on the wafer. The ball count is limited by die area: a 4 mm by 3 mm die at 0.4 mm pitch holds $\lfloor 4/0.4 \rfloor \times \lfloor 3/0.4 \rfloor = 10 \times 7 = 70$ balls. Fan-in is the smallest and cheapest package, ideal for small dies such as power management and radio parts. It has two limits. A large die puts far-from-centre balls under high thermal-mismatch strain against the board, and a small die with many I/O simply has no room. The second limit is what fan-out removes.

## Fan-out area expansion

If a die needs $B$ balls at pitch $p$ in a square full array, the package side must be at least $\lceil \sqrt{B} \rceil p$. A 5 mm by 5 mm die needing 400 balls at 0.4 mm pitch needs a $20 \times 0.4 = 8$ mm package, so the package area is $64/25 = 2.56$ times the die area. Fan-out WLP provides that extra area with mold compound around the die, and the RDL routes from die pads into it. Because the RDL is built with wafer-style lithography at a few micrometres line and space, fan-out also supports multi-die packages with fine die-to-die wiring and no laminate substrate, which is why it is used for application processors and for chiplet packages.

## Reconstituted wafers and panels

Fan-out starts by placing known-good dies on a carrier and overmolding them into a reconstituted wafer or a rectangular panel. Units are laid out at a step equal to package size plus a saw street, so a panel of $W_p \times H_p$ holds $\lfloor W_p/s \rfloor \times \lfloor H_p/s \rfloor$ units at step $s$. Panels raise throughput because a rectangle wastes less area on rectangular packages than a round wafer. Two process effects matter to a designer. Die shift: dies move slightly during molding, so the RDL lithography must align to each die's actual position, sometimes by adaptive patterning. Warpage: mold compound and silicon have very different CTEs, so the reconstituted wafer bows after cure, which limits panel size and RDL alignment.

lesson:
# Redistribution layers

A redistribution layer is a thin copper wiring level, insulated by polymer or inorganic dielectric, that moves connections from where the die's pads are to where the bumps or balls must be. RDLs appear in fan-in and fan-out WLP and on interposers. They are lithographically defined at a few micrometres line and space, far finer than a laminate substrate but far coarser than on-chip metal, and their resistance and density trade off directly.

## RDL trace resistance

An RDL trace of length $L$, width $w$ and thickness $t$ has $R = \rho L/(w t)$. With $\rho$ in micro-ohm cm, note that 1 micro-ohm cm is $10^{-2}$ ohm um, so with lengths in micrometres $R = 0.01 \rho L/(w t)$ ohms. Plated RDL copper is a little above bulk, around 2 micro-ohm cm. A 5 mm trace 5 um wide and 3 um thick has $R = 0.01 \times 2 \times 5000/15 = 6.67$ ohm. That is fine for a short signal into a high-impedance receiver but large for a long one, and the RC product with a few picofarads of load reaches tens of picoseconds. RDL thickness is the lever: thicker copper lowers resistance but makes fine line and space harder to pattern.

## IR drop on RDL power routes

Power often also travels through the RDL from a ball to the die's power pads, and the drop is $V = I R$. A power route of 2 ohm carrying 150 mA drops 300 mV, far too much for a 0.8 V supply whose budget might be a few percent. Designers therefore use wide RDL planes or meshes for power, many parallel paths, and place power balls close to the pads they feed. Because RDL copper is thin compared with substrate copper, an RDL-only package such as a substrate-less fan-out is more sensitive to IR drop and electromigration than a laminate package, and its power design is checked with the same grid analysis used on chip.

## Density against resistance

RDL density is $1000/(w+s)$ lines per millimetre per layer. Moving from a 10/10 um substrate-class pitch to a 2/2 um RDL gives $20/4 = 5$ times more wires per layer, so an edge that needed five substrate layers needs one RDL layer. The price is resistance: at fixed thickness-to-width ratio, resistance per unit length grows as the inverse square of the width. Fine RDL is therefore used for short, dense die-to-die wiring, while long or high-current routes stay on coarser layers. Multi-layer RDL stacks commonly combine a few fine layers near the die with coarser layers toward the balls, the same hierarchy logic as an on-chip metal stack.

## Going deeper

Lau, "Semiconductor Advanced Packaging" (2021), chapter on RDLs; Lau, "Fan-Out Wafer-Level Packaging" (2018).

lesson:
# System in package and multi-chip modules

A system in package (SiP) places several dies, often from different processes, and passive components in one package. A multi-chip module (MCM) is the older term for several bare dies on a shared substrate. Both trade the integration of one large die for assembly of several smaller ones. The central economic and engineering quantity is the yield of the assembled module, which multiplies the yields of every die and every assembly step.

## Compound module yield

If a module holds $k$ dies with yields $y_1, \ldots, y_k$ and each die attach succeeds with probability $y_a$, and these events are independent, the module yield is $Y = y_a^k \prod_i y_i$. Three dies at 0.95, 0.90 and 0.98 with a 0.99 attach yield give $0.99^3 \times 0.95 \times 0.90 \times 0.98 = 0.8131$, or 81.31%. Yield multiplies, so a module of many parts loses a lot even when each part is good, and one bad die scraps the whole module including the good dies already attached. This is the multiplication the whole field fights, and it is why dies are tested before assembly.

## Known-good die

Testing before assembly replaces each raw die yield with the probability that a die passing test is really good. If wafer test lets a fraction $e$ of bad dies escape among those shipped as good, each tested die is good with probability $1 - e$, and the module yield becomes $Y = \prod (1-e_i) \times y_a^k$. With four dies at 2% escape each and 0.995 attach, $Y = 0.98^4 \times 0.995^4 = 0.9041$. Known-good die (KGD) testing is hard because bare dies are probed at wafer level, often with limited speed and temperature coverage, so test escapes rather than raw defect yield often dominate module loss.

## Cost per good module

The cost of a good module is the cost of everything that went into all modules divided by the yield: $C_{good} = (\sum_i C_i + C_{asm})/Y$. With dies costing 20, 12 and 6 units, assembly 5 units and a module yield of 0.85, the cost per good module is $43/0.85 = 50.59$ units. The formula shows two levers: raise $Y$ by better KGD test, or make failures cheaper by assembling expensive dies last or by allowing rework. It also shows why SiP pays off: small dies from the best process for each function, a radio die and a logic die say, can cost less in total than one large die on the most expensive process, even after assembly loss.

## Going deeper

# 2.5D integration on interposers

In 2.5D integration several dies sit side by side on an interposer, a thin slab carrying fine wiring between them, which in turn sits on a package substrate. A silicon interposer uses back-end-of-line style wiring at about a micrometre pitch and through-silicon vias to reach the substrate. It gives die-to-die wiring thousands of times denser than a laminate, at the cost of a large silicon part that may exceed the lithography reticle.

## Interposer area and the reticle

An interposer must hold its dies, the gaps between them and an edge margin. For $k$ dies of width $W$ and height $H$ in a row with gap $g$ and margin $m$, the area is $(kW + (k-1)g + 2m)(H + 2m)$. A scanner exposes at most a 26 mm by 33 mm field, 858 mm^2. Two 25 by 30 mm dies with a 0.2 mm gap and 1 mm margin need $52.2 \times 32 = 1670.4$ mm^2, so at least $\lceil 1670.4/858 \rceil = 2$ reticle fields, stitched together. Stitching joins fields with matched wiring at the boundary; it is routine for interposers but adds design rules at the seams. Large interposers motivate the alternatives: organic interposers, and small silicon bridges.

## Wires across the die edge

The value of an interposer is wire density at the die edge. With wiring pitch $p$ and $N$ routing layers, the edge of length $E$ supports $N \lfloor E/p \rfloor$ wires. At 0.8 um pitch on 3 layers over 8 mm that is $3 \times 10000 = 30000$ wires. A laminate substrate at 20 um pitch on the same edge would carry 400 per layer. Interposer wires are short, usually a few millimetres, and are driven by simple unterminated drivers, which keeps energy per bit low. Their resistance, a few ohms per millimetre at sub-micrometre widths, limits reach to a few millimetres before repeaters or slower signalling are needed.

## The bump bottleneck

Wires on the interposer must land on the die through microbumps, and the bumps, not the wires, are usually the limit. If signal bumps occupy a band of depth $D$ along an edge of length $E$ at pitch $p_b$, the band holds $\lfloor E/p_b \rfloor \lfloor D/p_b \rfloor$ bumps. At 40 um pitch over 8 mm and a 1 mm band, that is $200 \times 25 = 5000$, far fewer than the 30000 wires the interposer could carry. The usable count is the minimum of the two. Raising bandwidth therefore means shrinking bump pitch, deepening the band at the cost of die area, or raising the data rate per wire. This is the motivation for hybrid bonding and for interface standards that fix bump maps.

## Going deeper

lesson:
# Embedded silicon bridges

An embedded silicon bridge is a small piece of silicon with fine wiring, placed only under the facing edges of two dies, inside an organic substrate or a mold layer. It gives die-to-die wire density close to a full silicon interposer where it is needed, while the rest of the package stays organic. The trade-offs are silicon area, assembly tolerance and the number of edges a bridge can serve.

## Silicon area saved

A full interposer covers the whole multi-die footprint, while bridges cover only the edge regions where dies talk. For a 1600 mm^2 interposer replaced by four bridges of 8 mm by 3 mm, the silicon area falls from 1600 to $4 \times 24 = 96$ mm^2, a ratio of about 16.7. Less silicon means lower cost and no reticle-size limit on the package, because each bridge is small. What is lost: the bridge provides no through-silicon vias, so power and other I/O reach the dies through the organic substrate at coarse pitch, and the full interposer's freedom to route between any two points on the footprint is gone. Bridges suit dies that talk mostly to neighbours.

## Wires per bridge

A bridge carries wires across the gap between two dies. If it spans an edge length $E$ under both dies with wiring pitch $p$ and $N$ layers, it carries $N \lfloor E/p \rfloor$ wires, and $n$ bridges carry $n$ times that. With a 6 mm edge, 2 um pitch, 2 layers and three bridges, total wires are $3 \times 2 \times 3000 = 18000$. The pitch is coarser than a full interposer's best, because the bridge is often built with relaxed rules to lower cost, but still far finer than organic wiring. As with any interposer, the microbumps over the bridge, not the bridge wires, usually set the usable count.

## Bandwidth through bridges

Bandwidth is wires times data rate. If 4000 signal wires per bridge each run at 4 Gb/s, one bridge carries 16 Tb/s, and three bridges 48 Tb/s. The design question is whether that matches the traffic between the dies. Bridges also impose assembly constraints: the bridge sits at a slightly different height and position than the substrate pads around it, so the bump heights and placement tolerances must absorb both, and the die must bond to the fine bridge bumps and the coarse substrate bumps in the same reflow. An EDA flow must model the bridge as a separate routing layer set with its own rules, and floorplan the dies so that the communicating edges face each other over a bridge.

## Going deeper

Mahajan and others, "Embedded multi-die interconnect bridge", IEEE ECTC (2016); Lau, "Semiconductor Advanced Packaging" (2021), chapter on bridges.

label: 3D ICs and TSVs
lesson:
# 3D ICs and TSVs

A 3D IC stacks dies vertically and connects them through the silicon with through-silicon vias (TSVs): copper-filled holes insulated by an oxide liner. TSVs give vertical connections tens of micrometres long instead of millimetres of lateral wire, but they occupy area, stress the surrounding silicon and require thinned dies. Their geometry, aspect ratio and resistance are the first things a 3D floorplanner must know.

## Aspect ratio and die thickness

A TSV is etched by deep reactive-ion etching to a depth equal to the thinned die thickness $t$. Etch, liner deposition and copper fill are reliable only up to an aspect ratio $AR = t/d$ of roughly 10, sometimes more. So for a 5 um diameter TSV the die can be at most about 50 um thick, and a 100 um thick die needs TSVs of at least 10 um diameter. This couples three choices: thin dies allow small TSVs and dense vertical wiring but are fragile and need carrier wafers during processing; thick dies are robust but force large TSVs. Via-middle TSVs, formed after front-end transistors and before the back-end stack, are common for logic stacking.

## TSV resistance

A copper TSV is a cylinder of length $t$ and diameter $d$, so $R = \rho t/(\pi d^2/4)$. With $\rho = 1.7$ micro-ohm cm, which is 0.017 ohm um, a 50 um long, 5 um wide TSV has area 19.63 um^2 and $R = 0.017 \times 50/19.63 = 0.0433$ ohm, about 43 milliohm. That is small next to a millimetre of lateral wire, which is why vertical paths are attractive for power and signals. But a power network through hundreds of TSVs must still be modelled, because each TSV also carries a current limit for electromigration, and the current crowds where the TSV meets the thin back-end metal.

## TSV area overhead

Each TSV costs area on every die it passes through: the via itself plus a landing pad, and on the active die a keep-out zone. If $N$ TSVs each take a landing square of side $s$, the overhead fraction is $N s^2 / A_{die}$. Twenty thousand TSVs with 10 um landing pads on a 100 mm^2 die cost $20000 \times 100$ um^2 $= 2$ mm^2, or 2%. The overhead is why 3D partitioning tools minimise vertical connections and cluster them into arrays, why TSVs are placed in dedicated regions rather than scattered, and why a fine-grain partition that needs millions of vertical connections is only practical with hybrid bonding or monolithic 3D, not TSVs.

## Going deeper

label: TSV keep-out zones
lesson:
# TSV keep-out zones

Copper expands about six times more than silicon per kelvin, so after the anneal and cool-down a TSV leaves residual stress in the silicon around it. That stress changes carrier mobility and so the speed of nearby transistors. Placement tools therefore apply a keep-out zone (KOZ) around each TSV where no cells, or no sensitive cells, may be placed. The KOZ size is a direct area cost and depends on how fast the stress decays.

## Blocked area per TSV

A placer usually models the KOZ as a square or circle around the TSV. With TSV diameter $d$ and keep-out distance $k$ measured from the TSV edge, a square blockage has side $d + 2k$ and area $(d+2k)^2$. A 5 um TSV with a 5 um KOZ blocks $15^2 = 225$ um^2, nine times the TSV's own square. This is why the KOZ, not the via, dominates the area cost of TSVs on an active die. A KOZ can be relaxed for cells that tolerate a few percent of speed change, or applied per device orientation, because the piezoresistive response of silicon differs between electrons and holes and with the transistor's direction relative to the TSV.

## Fraction of a block lost

Multiply the per-TSV blockage by the count and divide by the block area: $f = N (d + 2k)^2 / A$. Two thousand TSVs at 225 um^2 each in a 4 mm^2 block lose $450000/4000000 = 11.25\%$ of the area. That loss lowers placement density and lengthens wires, which can erase the wirelength benefit of going 3D. TSV arrays reduce the loss because neighbouring keep-out zones overlap when TSVs are clustered at small pitch, so ten TSVs in a row block much less than ten isolated TSVs. Placement-aware 3D flows therefore weigh TSV clustering against the longer lateral wires needed to reach a cluster.

## Sizing the keep-out from stress decay

For a long cylinder with a thermal misfit in an infinite plate, the classic Lamé solution gives radial and hoop stresses that fall as $(R/r)^2$ with distance $r$ from the axis, where $R$ is the TSV radius. If the stress at the TSV edge is $\sigma_0$ and transistors tolerate $\sigma_{th}$, the safe radius is $r = R\sqrt{\sigma_0/\sigma_{th}}$, and the KOZ measured from the edge is $r - R$. For $R = 2.5$ um, $\sigma_0 = 200$ MPa and $\sigma_{th} = 20$ MPa, $r = 2.5\sqrt{10} = 7.91$ um, a KOZ of 5.41 um. The square-law decay means that a tenfold tighter tolerance costs only about three times the radius, and the real field near the surface and liner differs, so foundries calibrate KOZ rules by measurement and finite-element models.

lesson:
# TSV capacitance and delay

A TSV is a copper cylinder inside an oxide liner inside silicon, which makes it a coaxial capacitor to the substrate. That capacitance, typically tens of femtofarads, loads every signal that crosses a die boundary and enters timing, power and signal-integrity models. Extraction tools model it with the coaxial formula as a first estimate, refined for the depletion region in the silicon around the liner.

## The coaxial capacitance

For a conductor of radius $r$ inside a liner of outer radius $r + t_{ox}$ and length $L$, the coaxial formula gives $C = 2\pi \varepsilon_0 \varepsilon_{ox} L / \ln((r+t_{ox})/r)$. With $\varepsilon_0 = 8.854 \times 10^{-3}$ fF/um and $\varepsilon_{ox} = 3.9$, a TSV with $r = 2.5$ um, $t_{ox} = 0.2$ um and $L = 50$ um has $C = 2\pi \times 8.854 \times 10^{-3} \times 3.9 \times 50 / \ln(2.7/2.5) = 10.85/0.0770 = 141$ fF. This is the oxide capacitance only. In reality a depletion region forms in the silicon around the liner and adds a series capacitance, so the effective value is lower and depends on bias and doping, which is why 3D extraction uses voltage-dependent TSV models.

## TSV RC delay

A driver of output resistance $R_d$ charging the TSV plus a receiver load $C_L$ gives a 50% delay of about $0.69 R_d (C_{TSV} + C_L)$, because the TSV's own resistance of tens of milliohms is negligible. One kilo-ohm times one femtofarad is one picosecond. A 2 kilo-ohm driver into a 141 fF TSV plus 10 fF of load gives $0.69 \times 2 \times 151 = 208$ ps. That is slow compared with a gate delay, so TSV signals use stronger drivers, and dense TSV arrays use smaller diameters, which shrink both $r$ and $L$ and with them the capacitance. Hybrid-bond pads, with much smaller capacitance, make die crossings cheaper again.

## Liner thickness as a design lever

Capacitance depends on liner thickness through the logarithm. Doubling the liner from 0.2 to 0.4 um at $r = 2.5$ um changes $\ln(2.7/2.5) = 0.0770$ to $\ln(2.9/2.5) = 0.1484$, cutting capacitance by a factor of 0.519. A thicker liner lowers delay and switching energy, but it shrinks the copper core if the hole size is fixed, and thick liners are harder to deposit uniformly in deep holes. The logarithm also explains why shrinking the TSV's radius at fixed liner thickness increases the ratio $(r+t)/r$ and reduces capacitance per unit length. These sensitivities are exactly what a technology-exploration tool sweeps when it chooses a TSV process for a 3D stack.

## Going deeper

Katti, Stucchi, De Meyer and Dehaene, "Electrical modeling and characterization of through silicon via for three-dimensional ICs", IEEE Transactions on Electron Devices (2010).

label: Microbumps
lesson:
# Microbumps

Microbumps are small solder-capped copper pillars, at pitches of roughly 25 to 55 um, that join dies to interposers, bridges or other dies. They are the workhorse of 2.5D and of TSV-based 3D stacks. Their density sets die-to-die bandwidth, their current limit sets how many must carry power, and their resistance enters power-integrity analysis.

## Bump density from pitch

On a square grid at pitch $p$, the bump density is $(1000/p)^2$ per square millimetre with $p$ in micrometres. At 40 um this is 625 per mm^2; at 55 um about 331; at 25 um, 1600. Compare 44 per mm^2 for a 150 um flip-chip bump. Density grows with the inverse square of the pitch, so every pitch step matters twice. Microbumps cannot shrink indefinitely: the solder volume falls with the cube of the size, so small bumps become intermetallic-dominated, wetting and bridging control get harder, and alignment tolerance becomes a large fraction of the pad. Below about 10 um pitch, bumpless hybrid bonding takes over.

## Power bumps from current limits

Each bump carries a maximum current, set by electromigration in the solder and the intermetallic layers at operating temperature. If a die draws $I$ amps through bumps each limited to $I_{max}$, it needs at least $\lceil I / I_{max} \rceil$ power bumps, and as many ground bumps. A die drawing 60 A with 0.1 A per bump needs 600 power and 600 ground bumps, before any margin for uneven current sharing. Current does not share evenly: bumps above high-activity regions carry more, so analysis must solve the power network to find the worst bump rather than divide the total. The power bumps then compete with signal bumps for the same area, which is why bump maps are planned early.

## Bump resistance

A microbump joint is roughly a cylinder of solder and intermetallic with height $h$ and diameter $d$, so $R = \rho h/(\pi d^2/4)$. Tin-silver solder has resistivity around 12 to 15 micro-ohm cm, close to ten times copper. A joint 15 um tall and 20 um wide at 13 micro-ohm cm, which is 0.13 ohm um, has $R = 0.13 \times 15/314.2 = 6.2$ milliohm. Copper pillars carry most of the height with low resistance, so the solder cap dominates the series resistance. Thousands of such joints in parallel give a small total, but the per-bump value matters for the current sharing that sets the electromigration limit.

## Going deeper

label: Hybrid bonding
lesson:
# Hybrid bonding

Hybrid bonding joins two dies or wafers face to face with no solder: polished dielectric surfaces bond directly, and recessed copper pads expand during an anneal to form metal joints. Because there is no solder to wet or bridge, the pitch can drop below 10 um and toward 1 um in wafer-to-wafer bonding. The result is interconnect density orders of magnitude above microbumps, limited mainly by alignment and surface flatness.

## Connection density

Density at pitch $p$ is $(1000/p)^2$ per mm^2. At 9 um pitch that is about 12346 per mm^2; at 3 um, 111111; at 1 um, a million. A 50 mm^2 overlap at 3 um pitch offers about 5.6 million connections. Such density changes the design question from whether to cross a die boundary to how to use the crossings: memory stacked on logic with direct per-bank connections, or logic split between dies at the block or even cell level. The bonding pads also have far lower capacitance than microbumps, so each crossing costs little energy. The fabrication cost is a near-perfectly flat surface from chemical-mechanical polishing and particle-free bonding.

## Gain over microbumps

Because density scales as $1/p^2$, the gain from microbumps at pitch $p_{mb}$ to hybrid bonding at $p_{hb}$ is $(p_{mb}/p_{hb})^2$. From 40 um to 9 um the gain is $(40/9)^2 = 19.8$; from 36 to 3 um, 144. A designer should translate this into bandwidth only with care: bandwidth equals connections times data rate, and dense hybrid-bond interfaces often run each wire slower, because simple low-swing drivers save energy. Still, area per connection falls so far that the die-to-die interface can shrink from a large edge PHY to a small fraction of the die, which is what enables fine-grained 3D partitioning.

## Overlay and pad overlap

At fine pitch, alignment error is a large fraction of the pad. Two square pads of side $a$ offset by $e_x$ and $e_y$ overlap over $(a - e_x)(a - e_y)$, a fraction $(a-e_x)(a-e_y)/a^2$ of the pad. With 2 um pads and a 0.3 um by 0.2 um offset, overlap is $1.7 \times 1.8/4 = 76.5\%$. Contact resistance rises as overlap falls, and if the pad offset brings copper close to a neighbour's pad, the dielectric gap shrinks and leakage or shorts follow. Pitch therefore scales with alignment capability. Die-to-wafer bonding has looser alignment than wafer-to-wafer bonding, which is why the finest pitches are reached wafer to wafer, and why design rules couple pad size, pitch and the bonder's overlay specification.

## Going deeper

Lau, "Semiconductor Advanced Packaging" (2021), chapter on hybrid bonding; Enquist and others, "Direct bond interconnect", IEEE 3DIC conference (2009).

prereqs: System in package and multi-chip modules
lesson:
# Chiplet disaggregation and yield

Disaggregation splits what would be one large die into several smaller chiplets, joined in a package. The main driver is yield: the probability that a die is free of killer defects falls exponentially with its area, so small dies waste less silicon per good system. The gain is offset by die-to-die interface area, assembly yield and package cost, and the trade-off is computed before any architecture is committed.

## Poisson yield of a large die

With killer defects scattered at random with density $D_0$ per unit area, the number on a die of area $A$ is Poisson with mean $A D_0$, and the die is good with probability $Y = e^{-A D_0}$. Keep units consistent: with $D_0$ per cm^2, convert the area from mm^2 by dividing by 100. A 600 mm^2 die at 0.1 defects per cm^2 has $Y = e^{-0.6} = 54.88\%$. The same process yields $e^{-0.15} = 86.07\%$ for a 150 mm^2 die. Real fabs fit clustered models such as negative binomial, which are less pessimistic for large dies, but the exponential is the standard first estimate and the one used here.

## Chiplet yield with interface overhead

Splitting the die into $k$ chiplets does not divide the area exactly: each chiplet needs die-to-die PHYs and duplicated infrastructure, an overhead fraction $o$ of its logic area. Each chiplet has area $a = A(1+o)/k$ and yield $e^{-a D_0}$. Splitting the 600 mm^2 design into four chiplets with 10% overhead gives $a = 165$ mm^2 and a yield of $e^{-0.165} = 84.79\%$. Chiplets are tested before assembly, so bad chiplets are discarded individually rather than taking three good ones with them. That independence is the point; the overhead is the price, and it grows with the number of cuts, so splitting into many tiny chiplets eventually loses.

## Silicon per good system

Compare the manufactured silicon needed for one good system. Monolithic: $A/Y_{mono}$. Chiplets with known-good-die testing: $k a / Y_{chip} = A(1+o)/Y_{chip}$. For the example, monolithic needs $600/0.5488 = 1093$ mm^2 and chiplets $660/0.8479 = 778$ mm^2, a ratio of 1.40 in favour of chiplets. This ignores assembly yield, package cost and test cost, all of which favour monolithic, and the performance and energy cost of crossing die boundaries. It also ignores the reuse benefit: a chiplet design can serve several products, and an I/O chiplet can stay on an older, cheaper process. Real decisions add those terms to the same comparison.

## Going deeper

lesson:
# Die-to-die interface choices

A die-to-die interface is the circuit and protocol that moves data between chiplets in one package. The design space runs from wide, slow, parallel interfaces over very short dense wires to narrow, fast serial links over longer package traces. The right choice depends on reach, the package technology, bandwidth per millimetre of die edge, energy per bit and latency, and it constrains the floorplan and the package.

## Parallel and serial interfaces

Parallel interfaces send many single-ended signals at moderate rates, forwarded with a clock, over wires a few millimetres long on an interposer, bridge or fine-pitch substrate. Because the wires are short and dense, they need no equalization or clock recovery, so they achieve low energy and latency. Serial SerDes links send fewer differential lanes at tens of gigabits per second each, with equalization and clock-data recovery, over longer reaches on ordinary organic substrates. They need fewer bumps but spend more energy per bit and add latency for serialization and recovery. The choice follows the package: dense advanced packaging favours wide parallel interfaces; a cheap laminate with coarse bumps favours serial links.

## Shoreline and reach

Die-to-die interfaces live on die edges, and edge length, the shoreline, is scarce: a die has four edges, and memory, I/O and other chiplets compete for them. The relevant figure of merit is bandwidth per millimetre of edge, which multiplies bump density, signal share and data rate. Reach matters because loss and crosstalk grow with wire length: a short unterminated parallel link stops working cleanly beyond a few millimetres, when transmission-line effects and RC attenuation take over and termination becomes necessary, which costs power. A floorplanner must therefore place communicating chiplets with facing edges close together, and a package designer must keep those routes short and on the finest layers.

## Protocol, latency and test

Above the electrical layer, an interface carries a protocol. Some interfaces map existing protocols such as PCIe or CXL onto the die-to-die link so that chiplets from different vendors interoperate; others carry a raw streaming protocol for one vendor's chiplets. Latency comes from serialization, clock-domain crossing, retry and protocol layers, and it matters for cache-coherent traffic far more than bandwidth does. Interfaces also need lane repair, because a single bad microbump among thousands should not scrap the package: spare lanes and remapping logic replace failed lanes found at assembly test. A tool designer must model these redundancy schemes, because they change the bump map and the netlist that verification sees.

lesson:
# Chiplets and UCIe

Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express (UCIe) is an open die-to-die interconnect standard. It specifies a physical layer, a die-to-die adapter and protocol mappings, so chiplets from different sources can be combined. A designer uses it as a set of fixed building blocks: modules of a defined lane count at a defined data rate, for standard or advanced packages. The arithmetic of lanes, rates and modules sets the bandwidth a chiplet edge can deliver.

## Lanes, rate and module bandwidth

UCIe organizes the physical layer into modules. The specification defines a standard-package module of 16 data lanes per direction for organic substrates and an advanced-package module of 64 lanes per direction for interposers and bridges, with data rates per lane from 4 up to 32 GT/s in its published versions. Raw bandwidth per direction is lanes times rate: an advanced module of 64 lanes at 16 GT/s carries $64 \times 16 = 1024$ Gb/s each way, before protocol overhead. A standard module at the same rate carries 256 Gb/s. The advanced module packs more lanes into a narrow edge because the microbump pitch is finer, which is the whole reason advanced packaging exists.

## Shoreline bandwidth

Modules are placed side by side along a die edge. If a module occupies $w$ um of edge, an edge of $E$ mm holds $\lfloor 1000E/w \rfloor$ modules, and the edge bandwidth is that count times the module bandwidth. With 500 um modules on a 10 mm edge, 20 modules at 1024 Gb/s give 20.48 Tb/s per direction. Dividing by the edge length gives the shoreline density, here about 2 Tb/s per millimetre. Modules can also be stacked in depth to raise bandwidth further at the cost of die area. These numbers drive architecture: an accelerator needing 40 Tb/s to a neighbouring chiplet needs two edges or a faster rate, and the floorplan must provide them.

## Sizing for a target

Bandwidth targets are often given in bytes per second, while link rates are in bits. To deliver $T$ TB/s per direction with modules of $B$ Gb/s, the module count is $\lceil 8000 T / B \rceil$. For 1.5 TB/s with 64-lane modules at 32 GT/s, $B = 2048$ Gb/s and the count is $\lceil 12000/2048 \rceil = 6$. Forgetting the factor of eight is the classic error. A real plan then adds protocol and retry overhead, reserves redundant lanes for repair, and checks power: every module draws power in proportion to its traffic, so the energy per bit becomes the next constraint, alongside the bump map the modules impose.

## Going deeper

The UCIe Consortium specification and white papers; Das Sharma and others, "Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express (UCIe): an open industry standard for innovations with chiplets at package level", IEEE Transactions on Components, Packaging and Manufacturing Technology (2022).

label: Energy per bit and link power
lesson:
# Energy per bit and link power

Energy per bit is the energy an interface spends to move one bit from one die to another, usually quoted in picojoules per bit. Multiplied by bandwidth it gives link power, which can rival the power of the logic it connects. It is the main reason heterogeneous integration favours short, dense, simple die-to-die links over off-package SerDes, and it is computed from wire and pad capacitance.

## Link power

Power is energy per bit times bit rate: $P = E_b \times BW$. One picojoule per bit at one terabit per second is one watt, since $10^{-12} \times 10^{12} = 1$. A 0.5 pJ/bit die-to-die link carrying 8 Tb/s draws 4 W. Count both directions if both are active. These watts add to the package's thermal budget and to its power-delivery current, and they sit at the die edge, so they also create local hot spots under the PHYs. Architects therefore budget link power with logic power, and data-movement-heavy designs such as accelerators can spend a large share of their power on moving data rather than computing.

## On-package against off-package

Off-package SerDes over a board or cable spends energy on equalization, clock recovery and driving lossy channels, typically several picojoules per bit, while short on-package parallel links can stay well below one picojoule per bit. Moving 4 Tb/s at 6 pJ/bit costs 24 W, and at 0.4 pJ/bit 1.6 W, saving 22.4 W. This saving, more than raw bandwidth, justifies putting memory and compute in one package. The comparison must be like for like: some quoted figures count only the PHY and others include the adapter and protocol logic, and quoted values come from different process nodes and reaches, so a designer computes them for the actual channel.

## Energy from capacitance

For a full-swing, unterminated link, the dominant energy is charging the wire, pads and receiver input. Each 0-to-1 transition draws $C V^2$ from the supply. With random data, a given bit is a 0-to-1 transition with probability one quarter, so the average energy per bit is $C V^2/4$. A channel of 150 fF at 0.75 V spends $150 \times 0.5625/4 = 21.1$ fJ per bit, or 0.021 pJ/bit for the wire alone; drivers, receivers, clocking and the adapter add more. The formula shows the levers: lower capacitance, from shorter wires and smaller pads such as hybrid bonds, and lower swing, which helps quadratically but needs more sensitive receivers.

## Going deeper

Horowitz, "Computing's energy problem", ISSCC (2014); Lau, "Chiplet Design and Heterogeneous Integration Packaging" (2023).

label: Package-board co-design
lesson:
# Package-board co-design

Package-board co-design treats die, package and board as one system. The ball map, the power delivery path and the high-speed channels cross all three, and a choice made in one level, such as a ball assignment, fixes constraints for the others. Three computations anchor the practice: how many balls power needs, what impedance the power network must meet, and how many parallel paths achieve a target inductance.

## Power ball count

Each ball carries a maximum current, set by electromigration and joule heating at the operating temperature, often a few hundred milliamps to an ampere depending on ball size. A rail drawing $I$ amps needs at least $\lceil I/I_{ball} \rceil$ supply balls and as many return balls. A 120 A core rail at 0.6 A per ball needs 200 power and 200 ground balls. On a package of a few thousand balls, power can take most of the map, which is why high-power packages assign the central region under the die to power and ground, keep signals on the outer rings for escape, and interleave power and ground to reduce loop inductance.

## Target impedance

A power delivery network keeps the supply within a ripple tolerance despite current transients. The target impedance is $Z_t = V \times r / \Delta I$, where $r$ is the allowed ripple fraction and $\Delta I$ the transient current step. For a 0.75 V rail with 3% ripple and a 50 A step, $Z_t = 0.75 \times 0.03/50 = 0.45$ milliohm. The network must stay below this impedance from DC to the frequencies where on-die capacitance takes over. The board and its voltage regulator cover low frequencies, package capacitors and planes cover the middle, and on-die decoupling covers the highest. Each level is designed against the same target, so the package designer must know the board's capability and the die's decap.

## Parallel paths and inductance

Above a few megahertz the network is limited by inductance, of the balls, vias and planes. If one ball-and-via path has inductance $L_1$, $N$ paths in parallel give roughly $L_1/N$, ignoring mutual inductance between them. Reaching 5 pH with 300 pH per path needs $\lceil 300/5 \rceil = 60$ paths. Mutual coupling between same-direction currents raises the effective value, while interleaving power and ground lowers it because opposing currents cancel each other's field, so real designs extract the network rather than divide. This is a co-design result: the package fixes the ball pattern, the board fixes the via pattern underneath, and only together do they meet the target.

## Going deeper

label: Heat conduction and Fourier's law
prereqs: Heat equation and separation of variables
lesson:
# Heat conduction and Fourier's law

Heat leaves a chip mainly by conduction through solids: silicon, solder, thermal interface material, lid and heat sink, before convection carries it away. Conduction obeys Fourier's law, the heat-flow analogue of Ohm's law, and its one-dimensional form gives the thermal resistance of every layer in a package. That resistance is the building block of all package thermal models.

## Fourier's law

Fourier's law states that heat flux is proportional to the temperature gradient: $q'' = -k\,\nabla T$, with thermal conductivity $k$ in W/(m K). In one dimension through a slab of thickness $L$ with faces at $T_1$ and $T_2$, the heat flow is $Q = k A (T_1 - T_2)/L$. The steady heat equation $\nabla \cdot (k \nabla T) + q''' = 0$ follows from energy conservation. Conductivities span four orders of magnitude: copper about 400, silicon about 150 at room temperature, solder around 50, thermal interface materials a few, mold compound and underfill below one, and silicon dioxide about 1.4. Low-conductivity layers, even thin ones, therefore dominate the heat path.

## Resistance of a layer

Rearranging gives the thermal resistance $R = \Delta T/Q = L/(k A)$, in K/W. With $L$ in micrometres and $A$ in mm^2 the factors of $10^{-6}$ cancel, so $R = L/(kA)$ directly. A 750 um silicon die of 100 mm^2 has $R = 750/(150 \times 100) = 0.05$ K/W; a 50 um interface layer at 4 W/(m K) over the same area has $50/400 = 0.125$ K/W, two and a half times the die's resistance despite being fifteen times thinner. At 100 W, the interface layer alone drops 12.5 K. This is why thermal interface materials and their bond-line thickness receive so much engineering attention.

## Sizing a material for a budget

The formula inverts to size a material: if a layer of thickness $L$ and area $A$ may drop at most $\Delta T$ while carrying $Q$, it needs $k \ge Q L/(A \Delta T)$. For 150 W through a 30 um bond line over 400 mm^2 with a 3 K budget, $k \ge 150 \times 30/(400 \times 3) = 3.75$ W/(m K). Two caveats. One-dimensional resistance assumes heat flows straight through; if the heat source is smaller than the layer, heat spreads, and the effective resistance is larger near the source and smaller far from it. And conductivity depends on temperature: silicon's falls as it heats, so hot dies conduct worse, a nonlinearity that full simulators include.

## Going deeper

label: Thermal resistance networks
lesson:
# Thermal resistance networks

A thermal resistance network models a package as resistors between temperature nodes, with power as current and temperature as voltage. Resistances add in series when heat flows through layers in turn and combine reciprocally when heat has parallel paths. With Kirchhoff's laws, the network gives every node temperature, and it is the compact model that system-level thermal tools exchange.

## Layers in series

When all heat flows through layers one after another, their resistances add: $R = \sum R_i$. A die at 0.05 K/W, an interface material at 0.1 K/W, a lid at 0.02 K/W, a second interface at 0.08 K/W and a heat sink at 0.25 K/W total 0.5 K/W. With 120 W the junction sits 60 K above ambient. The series view identifies the dominant resistance immediately: here the heat sink, then the two interface layers. Improving a layer that contributes 4% of the total cannot help much. The analogy is exact for steady state: temperature differences add like voltages and the same heat current flows through each layer.

## Parallel paths

When heat can leave by two paths, the resistances combine as $R = (1/R_1 + 1/R_2)^{-1}$. A die can lose heat upward through the lid and sink at 0.4 K/W and downward through bumps, substrate and board at 2.0 K/W, giving $1/(2.5 + 0.5) = 0.333$ K/W. The parallel result is always below the smaller resistance. Paths that look negligible still matter: the board path here lowers the junction temperature by 6.7 K at 100 W. In a mobile device with no heat sink, the board and the case may be the main paths, so the network depends on the product, not just the package.

## Heat split between paths

Parallel paths share the heat in inverse proportion to their resistance, exactly like current dividers. With top resistance $R_t$ and bottom $R_b$ from the same junction node to ambient, the fraction leaving through the bottom is $R_t/(R_t + R_b)$. For 0.4 and 2.0 K/W, $0.4/2.4 = 16.7\%$ leaves through the board. This split matters beyond temperature: board heat raises the temperature of neighbouring parts and of the solder joints, which feeds fatigue models. It also shows why a single junction-to-ambient number is not portable between boards, and why standards define two-resistor and multi-node compact models that keep the paths separate.

## Going deeper

label: Junction temperature and theta values
lesson:
# Junction temperature and theta values

Datasheets summarise package thermal behaviour with theta values: thermal resistances between the junction and a reference such as the ambient air, the case or the board, measured under standard conditions. Junction temperature then follows from power and theta, and so does the maximum power a part can dissipate. Knowing what each theta does and does not mean prevents the most common thermal design errors.

## Junction from power and theta

The junction temperature is $T_j = T_a + P\,\theta_{ja}$, where $\theta_{ja}$ is the junction-to-ambient resistance in K/W (often written °C/W). A 15 W part with $\theta_{ja} = 3.2$ K/W in 45 °C air runs at $45 + 48 = 93$ °C. The junction temperature is what matters for timing, leakage and reliability: leakage grows steeply with temperature, so a hot die burns more power and runs hotter still. $\theta_{ja}$ is measured on a standard test board in still or moving air, so it is a comparison figure. A real system with a different board, airflow or neighbours gives a different value.

## Maximum allowed power

Inverting gives the power budget: $P_{max} = (T_{j,max} - T_a)/\theta_{ja}$. With $T_{j,max} = 105$ °C, $T_a = 50$ °C and $\theta_{ja} = 2.5$ K/W, $P_{max} = 55/2.5 = 22$ W. This number flows back into the architecture: it bounds the frequency and voltage the chip can run at, and dynamic thermal management throttles the chip when sensors report the junction approaching the limit. Leakage feedback makes the true limit lower than the formula when leakage is a large share of power, because the power itself depends on temperature. A designer who uses typical ambient temperature instead of the worst case gets a budget that fails in the field.

## Case and sink resistances

With a heat sink, the path splits into junction-to-case $\theta_{jc}$, case-to-sink $\theta_{cs}$ through the interface material, and sink-to-ambient $\theta_{sa}$, in series: $T_j = T_a + P(\theta_{jc} + \theta_{cs} + \theta_{sa})$. At 80 W with 0.15, 0.1 and 0.4 K/W and 35 °C air, $T_j = 35 + 80 \times 0.65 = 87$ °C. $\theta_{jc}$ is measured with essentially all heat forced through the case top, so it is valid only when that path dominates. Datasheets also give characterisation parameters such as $\Psi_{jt}$, junction-to-top: these are not resistances of a path but ratios that let an engineer infer $T_j$ from a measured case-top temperature in a real system.

## Going deeper

JEDEC JESD51 series on thermal test methods; Lasance and Poppe, "Thermal Management for LED Applications" (2014), on theta and psi.

label: Power density and hot spots
lesson:
# Power density and hot spots

Power density is power per unit area, and its spatial variation, not the total power, decides the peak temperature on a die. Modern chips mix low-density caches with high-density arithmetic blocks, so the hottest spot can be many kelvin above the die average. Floorplanners, thermal sensors and throttling policies are all designed around hot spots, so computing them is a core package-chip co-design skill.

## Average power density

Average power density is $q'' = P/A$. A 300 W die of 6 cm^2 averages 50 W/cm^2. For scale, a kitchen hot plate is a few tens of W/cm^2, and high-performance processors exceed that on average and by several times locally. The unit conversion matters: W/mm^2 times 100 gives W/cm^2. Average density sets the heat-sink and package design, because the total heat must leave; but the cooling solution sized for the average does not guarantee the peak, because heat entering a small area must spread laterally before it reaches the large sink, and spreading has its own resistance.

## Hot-spot density ratio

A block with power $P_b$ over area $A_b$ has local density $P_b/A_b$, and its ratio to the die average measures how concentrated the heat is. A 40 W execution cluster on 25 mm^2 has 1.6 W/mm^2, or 160 W/cm^2, against a 50 W/cm^2 average, a ratio of 3.2. Hot-spot ratios of several times are common because activity is concentrated in arithmetic and register-file circuits. The ratio guides floorplanning: spreading hot blocks apart, interleaving them with cooler caches, and placing them under the best part of the heat-sink contact all lower the peak without changing total power.

## Temperature above the average

A simple vertical model gives each region a temperature rise of $q'' R''$, where $R''$ is an area-specific thermal resistance in K mm^2/W from that region to the coolant. With $R'' = 20$ K mm^2/W, a 0.5 W/mm^2 region rises 10 K and a 1.6 W/mm^2 hot spot rises 32 K, a 22 K difference. The vertical model overstates the hot spot, because lateral spreading in silicon and copper carries heat sideways; the smaller the hot spot, the more it spreads, so a tiny hot spot is cooler than this estimate. Thermal simulation captures spreading, and thinned dies in 3D stacks spread much less, which is why hot spots are worse in 3D.

## Going deeper

Skadron and others, "Temperature-aware microarchitecture", ISCA (2003); Incropera and others, "Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer", on spreading resistance.

label: Joule heating and self-heating
lesson:
# Joule heating and self-heating

Joule heating is the power $I^2 R$ dissipated when current flows through resistance. In packages it heats power bumps, balls, TSVs and planes; on chip it heats wires; and in transistors the channel's own power heats the device, called self-heating. Each local temperature rise feeds electromigration and resistance models, so even small heat sources matter for reliability signoff.

## Power in a conductor

A conductor of resistance $R$ carrying current $I$ dissipates $P = I^2 R$. A power bump of 6 milliohm carrying 0.15 A dissipates $0.0225 \times 0.006 = 0.135$ mW. Across thousands of bumps the total is modest, but a wire of 50 ohm carrying 2 mA dissipates 0.2 mW in a tiny volume. The quadratic dependence on current is the key: doubling current quadruples the heat, which is why current crowding at the entrance of a bump or via, where local current density is several times the average, produces local hot spots that limit electromigration lifetime.

## Temperature rise of a wire

A heat source of power $P$ connected to the substrate through thermal resistance $R_{th}$ rises $\Delta T = P R_{th}$. On-chip wires sit in low-conductivity dielectric, so their thermal resistance to the substrate can be large, thousands of K/W per wire segment. A segment dissipating 0.2 mW with 5000 K/W rises 1 K; one at 2 mW rises 10 K. Upper metal layers are farthest from the silicon, have the most dielectric beneath them, and carry the largest currents, so they heat most. Low-k dielectrics conduct heat worse than silicon dioxide, which makes wire heating worse as interconnect scales, and electromigration rules include a wire temperature that accounts for it.

## Transistor self-heating

A transistor dissipates $P = I_D V_{DS}$ in its channel. In planar bulk devices the heat flows easily into the substrate, but FinFETs and nanosheets are narrow structures surrounded by oxide, so their thermal resistance is higher and the channel runs hotter than the substrate. With $R_{th}$ in K per milliwatt, a device dissipating 200 uW with 30 K/mW rises 6 K. Self-heating lowers mobility and so drive current, and it raises the temperature seen by nearby wires and by aging models. Compact models such as BSIM include a self-heating thermal node, but they need the right $R_{th}$, which depends on layout and neighbours, a known modelling gap.

## Going deeper

Banerjee and Mehrotra, "Global (interconnect) warming", IEEE Circuits and Devices Magazine (2001); the BSIM-CMG manual on self-heating.

label: Thermal simulation
lesson:
# Thermal simulation

Thermal simulation solves the heat equation over the package and die to find the full temperature field, not just a few node values. The standard approaches discretize space by finite differences, finite volumes or finite elements, turning the partial differential equation into a large sparse linear system. Understanding the discretization explains the cost, the accuracy and the structure that fast solvers exploit.

## One Jacobi update

Discretize a uniform 1-D bar into nodes, each joined to its neighbours by a thermal resistance $R$. Energy balance at node $i$ with injected power $Q_i$ is $(T_{i-1} - T_i)/R + (T_{i+1} - T_i)/R + Q_i = 0$, so $T_i = (T_{i-1} + T_{i+1} + Q_i R)/2$. A Jacobi sweep updates every node from its neighbours' old values. With neighbours at 60 and 66 °C, $R = 2$ K/W and $Q_i = 1.5$ W, the update is $(60 + 66 + 3)/2 = 64.5$ °C. This is the finite-difference form of $k T'' + q''' = 0$, and it shows the method's character: each update is cheap and local, but information travels one node per sweep, so plain Jacobi converges slowly on fine grids.

## A chain with distributed heating

Exact solutions of small networks check a solver. Take $N$ nodes in a chain, the first joined to a sink at $T_s$ through resistance $R$, each joined to the next by $R$, with power $q$ injected at every node and an adiabatic far end. The link into node $k$ carries the heat of nodes $k$ to $N$, $(N - k + 1)q$, so the far-end rise is $R q \sum_{k=1}^{N} (N-k+1) = R q N(N+1)/2$. For $N = 6$, $R = 0.5$ K/W, $q = 2$ W and $T_s = 40$ °C, the far end is $40 + 0.5 \times 2 \times 21 = 61$ °C. Such closed forms are golden tests for a thermal solver.

## Grid size and sparsity

A 3-D finite-difference grid of $n_x n_y n_z$ cells gives one unknown per cell and a 7-point stencil: each row of the matrix has the node and up to six neighbours. The number of nonzeros is $N + 2[(n_x-1)n_y n_z + n_x(n_y-1)n_z + n_x n_y(n_z-1)]$, counting each neighbour link twice. A $100 \times 100 \times 10$ grid has $10^5$ unknowns and about $6.76 \times 10^5$ nonzeros. The matrix is symmetric positive definite, so conjugate gradient with a good preconditioner, or multigrid, solves it efficiently. Package-scale models reach millions of cells because thin layers need fine vertical resolution, which is why thermal tools use nonuniform meshes and model order reduction.

## Going deeper

Huang and others, "HotSpot: a compact thermal modeling methodology for early-stage VLSI design", IEEE Transactions on VLSI Systems (2006); Saad, "Iterative Methods for Sparse Linear Systems" (2nd ed., 2003).

label: Transient thermal response
lesson:
# Transient thermal response

Temperature does not respond instantly to power. Every material stores heat, which acts as a thermal capacitance, so a power step produces an exponential rise with a thermal time constant. Short power bursts may therefore exceed the steady-state power budget without overheating, which is the basis of boost and turbo modes, and transient models predict how long they can last.

## Thermal capacitance

A body of volume $V$, density $\rho$ and specific heat $c_p$ stores heat with capacitance $C_{th} = \rho c_p V$, in J/K. Silicon has $\rho = 2330$ kg/m^3 and $c_p \approx 700$ J/(kg K), so about 1.63 J/(cm^3 K). A 20 mm by 20 mm die 0.75 mm thick has $V = 0.3$ cm^3 and $C_{th} = 0.489$ J/K, or 489 mJ/K. Copper heat spreaders store more, about 3.45 J/(cm^3 K), and heat sinks far more. The capacitances of the layers form a ladder with the resistances, the thermal analogue of an RC line, and each stage contributes its own time constant.

## The thermal time constant

A single lumped body with capacitance $C_{th}$ and resistance $R_{th}$ to ambient responds with time constant $\tau = R_{th} C_{th}$, exactly like an electrical RC. The die above, with 0.489 J/K and a 0.2 K/W local path, has $\tau = 97.8$ ms. Real packages have time constants from microseconds (transistor and wire) through milliseconds (die) and seconds (spreader) to minutes (heat sink and chassis). Each power step excites all of them. A transient thermal model is therefore a network of several RC stages, often fitted from a measured step response, and its structure is what compact transient models exchange between vendors.

## Response to a power step

For a lumped body, a power step $P$ applied at $t=0$ gives $\Delta T(t) = P R_{th}(1 - e^{-t/\tau})$. With $P = 50$ W, $R_{th} = 0.2$ K/W and $\tau = 100$ ms, the final rise is 10 K, and after 50 ms the rise is $10(1 - e^{-0.5}) = 3.93$ K. After one time constant the rise is 63% of its final value, after three about 95%. This is why a chip can briefly run above its sustained power: during a short burst the die has not yet reached steady state. Boost control integrates exactly this response, often with a multi-stage model, to decide how long the burst may continue before the junction limit is reached.

## Going deeper

Incropera and others, "Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer", chapter 5 on transient conduction and the lumped capacitance method; JEDEC JESD51-14 on the transient dual interface method.

label: Thermal management: TIMs and heat sinks
lesson:
# Thermal management: TIMs and heat sinks

Thermal management is the set of materials and devices that move heat from the package to the environment: thermal interface materials (TIMs), lids and spreaders, heat sinks, fans, heat pipes, vapour chambers and liquid cooling. Each contributes a resistance to the path. The designer's job is to size these elements so that the junction stays below its limit at the worst-case power and ambient.

## Interface materials

Two solid surfaces touch only at asperities, leaving air gaps that conduct poorly. A TIM fills the gaps. Its resistance is $R = BLT/(kA)$ plus two contact resistances, where BLT is the bond-line thickness. A 40 um grease at 5 W/(m K) over 300 mm^2 gives $40/(5 \times 300) = 0.0267$ K/W, about 2.7 K at 100 W. Indium and liquid-metal TIMs conduct far better than greases; solder TIMs are used between a die and a lid in high-power parts. Bond-line thickness depends on surface flatness and clamping pressure, so warpage, which bends the die and lid apart, directly raises TIM resistance.

## Required heat-sink resistance

Given the power, the junction limit and the other resistances, the heat sink must satisfy $\theta_{sa} \le (T_{j,max} - T_a)/P - \theta_{jc} - \theta_{cs}$. For 150 W, a 95 °C limit, 40 °C air, $\theta_{jc} = 0.1$ and $\theta_{cs} = 0.05$ K/W, the budget is $55/150 - 0.15 = 0.217$ K/W. If no affordable sink meets it, the options are a better TIM, a lower $\theta_{jc}$ by a soldered lid or direct die contact, a lower ambient, or less power. This subtraction is how thermal requirements flow from the system to the package team, and why a package's $\theta_{jc}$ is a competitive number.

## Convection and fin area

A heat sink finally transfers heat to air by convection, with resistance $R = 1/(h A)$, where $h$ is the heat-transfer coefficient and $A$ the wetted area. Natural convection gives $h$ of a few to about 10 W/(m^2 K); forced air tens to about 100 or more; liquid cooling far higher. To reach 0.2 K/W with forced air at $h = 50$ W/(m^2 K) needs $A = 1/(50 \times 0.2) = 0.1$ m^2, 1000 cm^2, which is why sinks have many fins. Fin efficiency below one raises the needed area further. Liquid cold plates and immersion reach much lower resistances, which is why high-power accelerators move to liquid cooling.

## Going deeper

Incropera and others, "Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer", chapter 3 on extended surfaces; Prasher, "Thermal interface materials: historical perspective, status, and future directions", Proceedings of the IEEE (2006).

label: Thermomechanical stress from CTE mismatch
lesson:
# Thermomechanical stress from CTE mismatch

Every package joins materials that expand at different rates with temperature: silicon at about 2.6 ppm/K, copper near 17, organic substrates around 14 to 17, mold compounds from under 10 to over 20, and solder near 20. When the assembly is cooled from the temperature where it was bonded, or cycled in use, the mismatch becomes strain and stress. Those stresses drive warpage, joint fatigue, cracking and delamination, so they are computed from the first package concept onward.

## Mismatch strain

A free body of CTE $\alpha$ strains by $\alpha \Delta T$ when its temperature changes by $\Delta T$. Two bonded materials want different strains, and the difference $\Delta\alpha \Delta T$ is the mismatch strain that the bond must accommodate. Silicon on an organic substrate at 15 ppm/K, cooled 200 K from a solder reflow, has a mismatch of $12.4 \times 200 = 2480$ ppm, or 0.248%. That sounds small, but it is imposed over the whole bonded length and is comparable to the elastic strain limit of many materials. The reference temperature is the stress-free temperature, roughly where the bond solidified or the adhesive cured, not room temperature, which is why process history matters.

## Biaxial stress in a constrained film

If a thin layer is bonded to a much thicker, stiffer one, the layer is forced to take the substrate's strain, and the mismatch becomes stress in the layer. For an isotropic film in equal biaxial strain, $\sigma = \frac{E}{1-\nu}\Delta\alpha\Delta T$, where $E/(1-\nu)$ is the biaxial modulus. A copper film ($E = 120$ GPa, $\nu = 0.34$) on silicon with $\Delta\alpha = 14.4$ ppm/K cooled 100 K carries $120000/0.66 \times 0.00144 = 261.8$ MPa, beyond the yield stress of bulk annealed copper, so real films partly yield. The $1-\nu$ factor is the difference between a film constrained in two directions and a bar constrained in one, where $\sigma = E\Delta\alpha\Delta T$.

## Temperature swing to a stress limit

Inverting the film formula gives the temperature swing that reaches an allowable stress: $\Delta T = \sigma_{allow}(1-\nu)/(E\Delta\alpha)$. For a dielectric layer with $E = 70$ GPa, $\nu = 0.2$, $\Delta\alpha = 10$ ppm/K and a 300 MPa allowable stress, $\Delta T = 300 \times 0.8/(70000 \times 10^{-5}) = 342.9$ K, comfortably above a 200 K process swing. These simple formulas govern thin films far from edges. Near free edges and corners, stress concentrates and changes character, with peeling and shear components that drive delamination, so edge regions are always analysed with finite elements rather than the film formula.

## Going deeper

Freund and Suresh, "Thin Film Materials: Stress, Defect Formation and Surface Evolution" (2003); Suhir, "Structural Analysis in Microelectronic and Fiber-Optic Systems" (1991).
