lesson:
# CTE mismatch and warpage

Warpage is the out-of-plane bending of a package, wafer or panel caused by CTE mismatch between layers bonded at an elevated temperature. A warped package lifts its corner balls off the board during reflow, opens or bridges joints, raises thermal interface thickness and misaligns fine-pitch bonds. The bimaterial strip analysis of Timoshenko gives the curvature and is the first model every package mechanical engineer uses.

## Curvature of a symmetric bilayer

Two layers bonded stress-free and then cooled by $\Delta T$ bend toward the layer with the larger CTE, which shrinks more. Timoshenko's analysis gives the curvature $\kappa = 1/\rho$. When both layers have the same thickness and modulus, it reduces to $\kappa = 3\Delta\alpha\Delta T/(2h)$, with $h$ the total thickness. For $\Delta\alpha = 14$ ppm/K, $\Delta T = 100$ K and $h = 1$ mm, $\kappa = 3 \times 0.0014/0.002 = 2.1$ per metre, a radius of curvature of 0.476 m. Thinner stacks curve more, as $1/h$, which is why thin packages and thinned dies warp more than thick ones.

## Timoshenko's general formula

For layer thicknesses $t_1, t_2$, moduli $E_1, E_2$, $m = t_1/t_2$, $n = E_1/E_2$ and $h = t_1 + t_2$, Timoshenko's result is $\kappa = \frac{6\Delta\alpha\Delta T(1+m)^2}{h[3(1+m)^2 + (1+mn)(m^2 + 1/(mn))]}$. A 0.3 mm silicon die (130 GPa) on 0.5 mm of mold-like material (20 GPa) with $\Delta\alpha = 12.4$ ppm/K and $\Delta T = 100$ K gives $m = 0.6$, $n = 6.5$ and $\kappa = 2.22$ per metre, a radius of 0.45 m. The formula shows that a stiff thin layer on a compliant thick one bends the stack less than equal layers would, and that the curvature is linear in $\Delta\alpha\Delta T$, so it reverses sign when the assembly is heated past its stress-free temperature.

## From curvature to warpage

Package warpage is quoted as the out-of-plane deflection over a span, not as curvature. A spherical cap with curvature $\kappa$ over span $L$ deflects $\delta = \kappa L^2/8$ for small curvature. With $\kappa = 2.1$ per metre over a 20 mm span, $\delta = 2.1 \times 0.0004/8 = 105$ um. Board-assembly standards and coplanarity limits are often on the order of 100 um or less for large BGAs, so this package is at the edge. Warpage also changes with temperature through reflow, sometimes changing shape from concave to convex, which is why warpage is measured across the full reflow profile by shadow moiré, and why fine-pitch bonding needs flat, CTE-matched parts.

## Going deeper

# Solder joint fatigue

Solder joints between a die and a substrate, or a package and a board, are sheared every time the temperature cycles, because the two sides expand by different amounts. Repeated plastic shear grows cracks until the joint fails. The joint strain follows from geometry, and the Coffin-Manson relation turns strain into cycles to failure, so a designer can predict how package size, standoff height and underfill trade against lifetime.

## Shear strain in a joint

A joint at distance $DNP$ from the neutral point, the centre that does not move, sees the two sides slide past each other by $\Delta\alpha\Delta T \cdot DNP$. Spread over the joint height $h$, the shear strain is $\gamma = \Delta\alpha\Delta T \cdot DNP/h$. A silicon die on a 17 ppm/K substrate ($\Delta\alpha = 14.4$ ppm/K), a 100 K swing, a corner joint 10 mm from centre and a 100 um standoff give $\gamma = 14.4 \times 10^{-6} \times 100 \times 10/0.1 = 0.144$, a huge 14.4%. Such strain would fail an unprotected joint within a few cycles, which is why flip chip on organic substrates uses underfill: the epoxy couples die and substrate so that the joints no longer carry the full mismatch.

## Coffin-Manson scaling

The Coffin-Manson relation says plastic strain range and cycles to failure follow a power law, $N_f \propto \gamma^{-n}$, with $n$ often near 2 for solders in simple models. So the ratio of lifetimes at two strains is $N_2/N_1 = (\gamma_1/\gamma_2)^n$. Raising strain by 1.5 times at $n = 2$ cuts life to $1/2.25 = 0.444$ of its previous value. The exponent is fitted from accelerated thermal cycling, and models such as Engelmaier's add dependence on cycle frequency and mean temperature. The power law makes the corner joints, with the largest DNP, fail first, so they are often made non-critical or depopulated.

## Geometry levers for life

Because $\gamma \propto DNP/h$ and $N_f \propto \gamma^{-n}$, life scales as $(h/DNP)^n$. A joint that lasts 2000 cycles at 10 mm DNP lasts $2000 \times (10/14)^2 = 1020$ cycles at 14 mm on a larger package, other things equal. Taller joints help, as do smaller packages, smaller temperature swings and better CTE matching. Accelerated test cycles, for example between about -40 and 125 °C, are translated to field conditions with an acceleration factor from the same model. In practice the simple shear formula overstates strain when the package and board bend, so finite-element models calibrate the strain while Coffin-Manson remains the life law.

## Going deeper

lesson:
# Finite element analysis of packages

Finite element analysis (FEA) solves the equations of elasticity, and often plasticity and creep, over a meshed model of the package. It is the tool that predicts warpage, joint strain, die stress and delamination risk where closed-form models fail: at edges, corners, non-uniform layers and nonlinear materials. For a tool designer the important questions are what the model includes, how it is meshed and loaded, and how its answers can mislead.

## Modelling choices

A package FEA model starts with geometry, materials and loads. Geometry is simplified: thousands of solder joints are often replaced by a homogenized layer except in a submodel of the critical corner joints. Materials need temperature-dependent moduli and CTEs, plus nonlinear behaviour: solder creeps at room temperature, mold compound and underfill are viscoelastic and change sharply at their glass transition temperature. The load is a temperature history starting from the stress-free state, not a single temperature. Symmetry is used to model a quarter or an eighth of the package when geometry and loads allow, cutting the cost. Each simplification is a choice that must be justified against what the analysis must predict.

## Mesh, elements and convergence

FEA discretizes displacement with elements: bricks or tetrahedra in 3-D, shells for thin layers. Thin layers such as die-attach films and RDL dielectrics are hard to mesh because elements must stay well shaped while being very thin, so analysts use layered shell or solid-shell elements, or many thin bricks. Accuracy is checked by refining the mesh and confirming that the quantity of interest converges. At sharp re-entrant corners between bonded materials, linear elasticity predicts a stress singularity, so the peak stress keeps rising with refinement and never converges. Analysts then compare quantities that do converge, such as stress at a fixed distance or an energy release rate, rather than the peak value.

## Validation and use in the flow

FEA results must be validated against measurements: warpage across the reflow profile from shadow moiré, strain from digital image correlation, and cycles to failure from thermal cycling. A model calibrated this way can then explore designs faster than building them. In an EDA flow, FEA is the accurate engine: chip-package interaction checks use it to map stress from bumps into the die's back-end stack, and warpage simulation guides substrate stackups. Because full models are slow, tools build reduced models or surrogates from FEA runs, and the main risk is using a surrogate outside the range of designs it was fitted on.

## Going deeper

lesson:
# Electromigration and Black's equation

Electromigration is the slow transport of metal atoms by the momentum of conducting electrons. Over years it opens voids that break wires or raise their resistance, and pushes metal into hillocks that short to neighbours. Black's equation relates the median time to failure to current density and temperature, and it is the basis of the current-density rules that power grids, bumps and TSVs are signed off against.

## Current density

Electromigration depends on current density $J = I/A$, not current. A copper line 1 um wide and 0.5 um thick carrying 10 mA has $J = 0.01/(0.5 \times 10^{-8}$ cm^2$) = 2 \times 10^6$ A/cm^2, or 2 MA/cm^2. Units matter: one square micrometre is $10^{-8}$ cm^2. In packages the cross-sections are large but so are currents: a 20 um microbump at 0.2 A carries about 64000 A/cm^2, and solder fails at much lower current density than copper because tin diffuses fast. Current crowding where a narrow line enters a wide bump raises the local density several times above the average, which is why bump EM is analysed with detailed models.

## Black's equation

Black's equation states $MTTF = A J^{-n} e^{E_a/(kT)}$, where $n$ is the current exponent, $E_a$ the activation energy and $k$ Boltzmann's constant. At fixed temperature, changing current density from $J_1$ to $J_2$ scales life by $(J_1/J_2)^n$. With $n = 2$, a design that lasts 15 years at 1.5 MA/cm^2 lasts $15 \times (1.5/2)^2 = 8.44$ years at 2 MA/cm^2. The exponent is close to 2 when void nucleation limits life and close to 1 when void growth does, so the choice matters when extrapolating. EM signoff turns a target lifetime and temperature into a maximum allowed $J$ per wire width and layer, which the power-grid tool checks for every segment.

## Allowed current for a lifetime

Inverting at fixed temperature gives the current density allowed for a target life: $J_2 = J_1 (MTTF_1/MTTF_2)^{1/n}$. If a line reaches 5 years at 3 MA/cm^2 and must last 10 years with $n = 2$, the allowed density is $3/\sqrt{2} = 2.121$ MA/cm^2. Multiplying by the cross-section gives the allowed current, and so the wire width a power route needs. EM limits are statistical: Black's equation gives a median, and failure distributions are lognormal, so signoff uses a failure fraction far below 50%, which lowers the allowed density further. The limits differ for DC power current and for bidirectional signal current, which partly heals.

## Going deeper

label: EM temperature acceleration and Blech length
lesson:
# EM temperature acceleration and Blech length

Electromigration accelerates strongly with temperature through the Arrhenius factor in Black's equation. Reliability engineers exploit this to test in days what happens over years, and designers must account for it, because the local wire temperature, including Joule heating, sets the life. Short lines can also be immune: the Blech effect makes lines below a critical length-current product stop failing.

## Arrhenius acceleration

At fixed current density, the ratio of lifetimes at two absolute temperatures is $AF = \exp\left(\frac{E_a}{k}\left(\frac{1}{T_{use}} - \frac{1}{T_{stress}}\right)\right)$, with $k = 8.617 \times 10^{-5}$ eV/K. For copper with $E_a = 0.85$ eV, a 105 °C use condition (378.15 K) and a 300 °C stress (573.15 K) give $AF = \exp(9864 \times 0.0009) \approx 7150$. Temperatures must be in kelvin. The large factor is what makes accelerated tests possible, but it also means a 10 K error in the use temperature changes predicted life by tens of percent, so Joule heating of the wire itself must be included.

## Extrapolating a stress test

Combining current and temperature, the use life is $MTTF_{use} = MTTF_{stress} (J_s/J_u)^n \cdot AF$. A test at 3 MA/cm^2 and 300 °C fails at a median of 200 hours. At 1.5 MA/cm^2 and 105 °C with $n = 2$ and the factor 7150, the median use life is $200 \times 4 \times 7150 = 5.72$ million hours, about 653 years. That seems huge, but the design target is the time to a small failure fraction across millions of lines, not the median of one, which brings the margin down by orders of magnitude. The extrapolation also assumes that the same failure mechanism operates at test and use conditions.

## The Blech length

In a line blocked at its ends by diffusion barriers, electromigration builds a back-stress gradient that pushes atoms the other way. If the line is short enough, the back stress balances the electron wind and net transport stops. The criterion is a product: lines with $jL < (jL)_c$ are immortal, with a threshold of the order of a few thousand A/cm for copper, depending on the dielectric and cap. At $j = 2$ MA/cm^2 and $(jL)_c = 3000$ A/cm, the critical length is $3000/(2 \times 10^6) = 1.5 \times 10^{-3}$ cm, or 15 um. EM checkers use the Blech effect to waive short segments, and designers deliberately break long power straps into short segments between vias.

label: Stress migration and voiding
lesson:
# Stress migration and voiding

Stress migration, also called stress-induced voiding, moves metal atoms under a gradient of mechanical stress rather than electron current. Copper lines and vias embedded in dielectric are left in tension after processing, because copper shrinks more than its surroundings on cooling, and vacancies diffuse toward stress concentrations, often under vias, until a void opens. It is a failure mechanism with no current at all, and it has a peculiar temperature dependence.

## Mechanism and driving force

After copper is deposited and annealed, it cools inside a dielectric and barrier that expand much less. The copper ends in hydrostatic tension, and the tension is not uniform: it is highest where geometry concentrates it, such as under a via landing on a wide line. Atoms diffuse from regions of high tensile stress, which is equivalent to vacancies diffusing toward them, and vacancies collect into a void at the weakest interface. Wide lines provide a large reservoir of vacancies, so a via on a wide plate is more vulnerable than a via on a narrow line, the opposite of the intuition from electromigration.

## The temperature peak

Stress migration is slowest at both temperature extremes. Near the stress-free temperature, which is near the process anneal, the driving stress vanishes. At low temperature the stress is large but diffusion is frozen. The product of driving force, rising as temperature falls below the stress-free point, and diffusivity, falling as temperature falls, peaks in between, typically in a band around 150 to 250 °C for copper interconnect. Qualification therefore bakes parts at several temperatures to find the peak instead of assuming that hotter is always worse. This is a key difference from electromigration and dielectric breakdown, which accelerate monotonically with temperature.

## Design and verification response

Designers fight stress voiding with redundant vias, which give a second path when one opens, and with layout rules that limit the width of lines landing on single vias or add slots to wide plates. Verification tools check these rules: a via-doubling check flags single vias on wide lines, and some flows compute a vulnerability score from the plate area feeding each via. In packages and 3D stacks the stress field also includes TSV and bump stress, so chip-package interaction analysis maps package stress into the back-end stack. Thermal cycling then combines with the residual tension, which is why stress migration is often qualified alongside thermal-cycle tests.

lesson:
# Time-dependent dielectric breakdown

Time-dependent dielectric breakdown (TDDB) is the gradual degradation of an insulator under an electric field until a conductive path forms and it shorts. It limits gate oxides, the low-k dielectric between closely spaced copper lines, the liners of TSVs and the dielectrics of hybrid bonds. Lifetime models in field and Weibull statistics in area let engineers extrapolate from accelerated tests to use conditions and to the full chip.

## The electric field

The field across a dielectric of thickness $t$ at voltage $V$ is $E = V/t$. A useful conversion: 1 V across 1 nm is $10^7$ V/cm, or 10 MV/cm. So 0.8 V across 2 nm of gate dielectric is 4 MV/cm, and 0.75 V across 15 nm of low-k between lines is 0.5 MV/cm. Low-k dielectrics break down at far lower fields than thermal oxide, and they are porous and damaged by etch, so line-to-line TDDB becomes a limit as spacing shrinks. In hybrid bonding, pad misalignment shrinks the dielectric gap between a pad and its neighbour, which raises the field and makes overlay a reliability parameter as well as a yield one.

## Field acceleration models

Lifetime falls steeply with field. The E-model takes time to failure as $t_f \propto e^{-\gamma E}$, so the ratio between a use field $E_u$ and a stress field $E_s$ is $e^{\gamma(E_s - E_u)}$. With $\gamma = 2$ cm/MV, stressing at 8 MV/cm and using at 5 MV/cm gives a factor $e^{6} = 403$. Other models are used too: a $1/E$ model, power-law voltage models for thin gate oxides, and the square-root-of-E model proposed for low-k. They agree at stress conditions but diverge by orders of magnitude when extrapolated to low use fields, so the model choice is itself a reliability decision and must be justified by data across several stress fields.

## Weibull statistics and area scaling

Breakdown times follow a Weibull distribution with shape $\beta$ and characteristic life $\eta$. Because breakdown is a weakest-link event, a larger area fails sooner: $\eta_2 = \eta_1 (A_1/A_2)^{1/\beta}$. A test structure of 1 unit area with $\eta = 10$ years scaled to a chip with 100 times the area and $\beta = 1.5$ gives $10 \times 0.01^{1/1.5} = 0.464$ years for the chip's characteristic life. That is why a chip with many metres of minimum-spaced lines needs a much larger per-line margin than a test structure suggests. Low $\beta$, typical of thin and defective dielectrics, makes area scaling harsher.

## Going deeper

McPherson, "Reliability Physics and Engineering" (3rd ed., 2019).

prereqs: Bias temperature instability and hot carriers
lesson:
# Aging and lifetime guard bands

Aging is the slow drift of transistor parameters over a product's life, chiefly threshold voltage shifts from bias temperature instability and hot-carrier injection. Their effect on circuits is slower gates, so a design must carry a guard band in timing so that it still meets frequency at end of life. Package temperature drives the rate, which connects thermal design to timing signoff.

## Power-law threshold shift

Bias temperature instability shifts threshold voltage roughly as a power of stress time, $\Delta V_{th} = A t^n$, with $n$ often between about 0.1 and 0.25. So the shift at a later time is $\Delta V_{th}(t_2) = \Delta V_{th}(t_1)(t_2/t_1)^n$. A 15 mV shift after 1000 hours of stress, extrapolated to 10 years (87600 hours) with $n = 0.2$, gives $15 \times 87.6^{0.2} = 15 \times 2.45 = 36.7$ mV. The small exponent means most of the shift happens early, which is why burn-in captures a large part of it. BTI also partly recovers when stress is removed, so duty cycle and the measurement delay affect the observed value.

## Time to a shift limit

Inverting the power law gives the time to reach an allowed shift: $t = t_1(\Delta V_{lim}/\Delta V_1)^{1/n}$. For a 50 mV limit, the example's 15 mV at 1000 hours and $n = 0.2$ give $1000 \times (50/15)^5 = 411500$ hours, about 47 years. The exponent $1/n$ is large, so small changes in the measured shift or the exponent change the answer a lot, the same fragility as any long extrapolation. Temperature accelerates BTI through an Arrhenius-like factor in $A$, so a package that runs 15 K hotter reaches the limit much sooner. That is the coupling to thermal design.

## Delay guard bands

Threshold shift slows gates. In the alpha-power model, delay scales as $1/(V_{DD} - V_{th})^{\alpha}$, with $\alpha$ between 1 and 2 for short-channel devices. The relative delay after aging is $((V_{DD} - V_{th0})/(V_{DD} - V_{th0} - \Delta V_{th}))^{\alpha}$. At 0.75 V supply, 0.3 V threshold, 30 mV shift and $\alpha = 1.3$, this is $(0.45/0.42)^{1.3} = 1.094$, a 9.4% slowdown. Signoff adds this as an aging guard band, either a flat derate or aged cell libraries characterized at end-of-life conditions. A guard band that is too small fails in the field, and one that is too large wastes frequency on every part.

## Going deeper

lesson:
# Electro-thermal multiphysics coupling

Electrical, thermal and mechanical behaviour are coupled. Current heats conductors, heat raises resistance, higher resistance changes the heat, and temperature drives both stress and electromigration. A multiphysics simulation solves these fields together, either in one monolithic system or by iterating between single-physics solvers. The simplest case, a resistor heating itself, shows how the coupling converges, and how it can run away.

## Iterating the coupling

A conductor with resistance $R(T) = R_0(1 + \beta(T - T_0))$ carries current $I$ and has thermal resistance $\theta$ to an ambient $T_a$, with $T_0 = T_a$. Its temperature satisfies $T = T_a + \theta I^2 R(T)$. Fixed-point iteration alternates the two solvers: compute power from the current temperature, then temperature from the power. With $R_0 = 0.05$ ohm, $I = 3$ A, $\theta = 40$ K/W, $\beta = 0.0039$ per K and $T_a = 50$ °C, iteration one gives $50 + 40 \times 9 \times 0.05 = 68$ °C, and iteration two uses $R = 0.05(1 + 0.0039 \times 18) = 0.0535$ ohm to give 69.26 °C. This loose coupling is how many tools combine an electrical and a thermal solver.

## The converged temperature

Because the equation is linear in $T$, it has a closed form. With $T_0 = T_a$, the rise is $\Delta T = \theta I^2 R_0/(1 - g)$, where $g = \theta I^2 R_0 \beta$ is the loop gain. In the example $g = 40 \times 9 \times 0.05 \times 0.0039 = 0.0702$ and $\Delta T = 18/0.9298 = 19.36$ K, so the converged temperature is 69.36 °C. The iteration converges because $g < 1$, and its error shrinks by a factor $g$ each step, so after two steps it is within 0.1 K. That rate is the general lesson: loose coupling converges fast when the coupling is weak and slowly when it is strong, when a monolithic Newton solve is better.

## Thermal runaway

When the loop gain reaches 1, the denominator vanishes and there is no steady state: each degree of heating adds more than a degree, and the temperature runs away until something melts or a limit intervenes. The critical current is $I_c = 1/\sqrt{\theta R_0 \beta}$; for the example $1/\sqrt{40 \times 0.05 \times 0.0039} = 11.32$ A. Real systems include other feedbacks: leakage power grows exponentially with temperature, so a chip can run away even when wire heating is benign. Multiphysics signoff checks that the coupled solution exists and converges with margin, because a solver that stops after a fixed number of iterations can report a plausible temperature for a system that has no steady state.

## Going deeper

lesson:
# Partitioning a design across dies

A 3D or multi-die design must be partitioned: each cell or block is assigned to a die so that the vertical connections stay within budget while area, power and timing balance. This is a hypergraph partitioning problem with die-specific constraints, solved by the same min-cut machinery used in placement, Fiduccia-Mattheyses moves and multilevel coarsening, but with costs that reflect TSVs, bumps or bond pads.

## Cut nets between two dies

Model the netlist as a hypergraph: cells are vertices and each net is a hyperedge joining its cells. Given an assignment of cells to dies, a net is cut when its cells sit on more than one die, and each cut net needs at least one vertical connection. For nets $\{a,b\}$, $\{b,c,d\}$, $\{a,e\}$ and $\{d,e\}$ with $a, b$ on die 0 and $c, d, e$ on die 1, the cut nets are $\{b,c,d\}$, $\{a,e\}$, so the cut is 2 (the net $\{d,e\}$ is internal to die 1). Minimizing the cut subject to area balance is NP-hard, which is why practical tools use multilevel heuristics.

## Vertical connections in a stack

In a stack of more than two dies, a net touching die 0 and die 2 must pass through die 1, so it needs a connection at each interface it crosses. Number the dies by height; a net spanning dies from $d_{min}$ to $d_{max}$ needs $d_{max} - d_{min}$ vertical connections in a simple model with one connection per interface. The total is the sum over nets. This makes the objective sensitive to which dies communicate: putting two heavily connected blocks on non-adjacent dies costs twice. Face-to-face bonding of the two most connected dies, with TSVs only to the others, is a common response.

## Move gain

Iterative improvement moves one cell at a time to the other die and keeps moves that lower the cut. The gain of moving a cell is the cut before the move minus the cut after. Moving cell $e$ from die 1 to die 0 in the example affects only its nets: $\{a,e\}$ becomes internal to die 0, saving one, while $\{d,e\}$ becomes cut, costing one, so the gain is 0. Fiduccia and Mattheyses compute such gains for all cells, keep them in bucket lists for constant-time selection, and lock moved cells to avoid cycling. Area balance limits which moves are legal, and 3D tools add timing and thermal terms to the gain.

## Going deeper

Fiduccia and Mattheyses, "A linear-time heuristic for improving network partitions", DAC (1982); Lim, "Design for High Performance, Low Power, and Reliable 3D Integrated Circuits" (2013).

label: Inter-die timing
lesson:
# Inter-die timing

A timing path that crosses dies passes through drivers, bumps or TSVs, and receivers, and its launch and capture clocks are distributed by separate clock trees on separate dies. The dies may come from different wafers, lots or even processes, so their variations are independent. Inter-die timing analysis must model the crossing delay, the clock latency on each die and the corner combinations that independence creates.

## Setup slack across a die boundary

Setup slack is the required time minus the arrival time. For a path launched on die A and captured on die B, the arrival is the launch clock latency $L_A$ plus the launch-die logic, the crossing (driver, bump or TSV, receiver) and the capture-die logic. The required time is the period plus the capture latency $L_B$ minus setup. With a 1000 ps period, $L_A = 300$, $L_B = 340$, 380 ps of logic on die A, 90 ps crossing, 260 ps on die B and 30 ps setup, the slack is $1000 + 340 - 30 - (300 + 380 + 90 + 260) = 280$ ps. Each die's clock tree is separate, so the difference $L_B - L_A$ is a skew that a die-level analysis alone never sees.

## Independent die corners

Dies made on different wafers do not share a process corner, so a path can see a slow launch die and a fast capture die. If die delays scale by $k_A$ and $k_B$, a single-corner analysis that assumes both dies slow overstates the delay of the capture-die logic by $(k_{slow} - k_B)$ times its delay. With 260 ps of capture-die logic, a slow factor of 1.15 and an actual capture factor of 0.9, the pessimism is $0.25 \times 260 = 65$ ps. Correct analysis enumerates corner combinations per die, which grows as the number of corners to the power of the number of dies, or uses statistical timing with independent die-level variables. Tools prune combinations that cannot be worst.

## Hold across dies

Hold checks need the earliest arrival and the latest capture clock. Hold slack is the minimum arrival minus the capture clock latency minus the hold time, all measured from the same edge: $\text{slack} = (L_A + d_{min}) - (L_B + t_{hold})$. With $L_A = 300$ ps, a minimum data delay of 95 ps including a fast crossing, $L_B = 380$ ps and 20 ps hold, the slack is $395 - 400 = -5$ ps, a violation. Skew between independently built clock trees on two dies is the usual cause, which is why 3D clocking either distributes one clock through dedicated vertical connections with matched delays, or retimes crossings through FIFOs or source-synchronous interfaces that tolerate skew.

## Going deeper

Lim, "Design for High Performance, Low Power, and Reliable 3D Integrated Circuits" (2013), chapters on 3D timing; Visweswariah and others, "First-order incremental block-based statistical timing analysis", DAC (2004).

problems.q: A path launches on die A and captures on die B. Clock period 1400 ps; launch clock latency on die A 250 ps; capture clock latency on die B 400 ps. label: Thermal-aware 3D floorplanning
lesson:
# Thermal-aware 3D floorplanning

In a 3D stack, dies far from the heat sink must push their heat through the dies nearer to it, and thinned dies spread heat poorly. Thermal-aware floorplanning decides which die goes where in the stack and where hot blocks sit within each die, so that peak temperature stays in budget. Simple resistance models make the trade-offs computable inside a floorplanner's inner loop.

## Peak temperature of a stack

Model a two-die stack with the heat sink above: ambient connects through $R_s$ to die A, next to the sink, and die A connects through $R_b$ to die B, farther away. All heat passes through $R_s$, and die B's heat also passes through $R_b$. So $T_A = T_a + (P_A + P_B) R_s$ and $T_B = T_A + P_B R_b$. With $P_A = 20$ W, $P_B = 60$ W, $R_s = 0.4$ K/W, $R_b = 0.3$ K/W and 40 °C ambient, $T_A = 72$ °C and $T_B = 90$ °C. The far die is the hottest whenever it dissipates power, and every watt in it heats the near die too.

## Ordering dies in the stack

Swapping the dies changes only the second term: the peak becomes $T_a + (P_A + P_B)R_s + P_{far} R_b$. Putting the 60 W die next to the sink and the 20 W die far gives a peak of $72 + 20 \times 0.3 = 78$ °C instead of 90, a 12 K reduction for the same total power. The rule is to put the high-power die nearest the sink, which often means logic near the sink and memory farther, but the electrical design may prefer the opposite order, for example to give the logic die direct access to package bumps. The floorplanner must weigh both, and thermal TSVs or dummy bumps can lower $R_b$ when the order is fixed.

## Lateral placement of hot blocks

Within a die, blocks heat each other. A compact model writes each block's temperature as $T_i = T_a + R_{ii} P_i + \sum_j R_{ij} P_j$, where $R_{ij}$ is the mutual thermal resistance, falling with distance. For two 10 W blocks with $R_{ii} = 2$ K/W, the mutual term is 0.8 K/W when adjacent and 0.2 K/W when separated, so the peak falls from $T_a + 28$ to $T_a + 22$, a 6 K gain from placement alone. Thermal-aware floorplanners add peak temperature from such models to wirelength and area in their cost function. In 3D, the mutual resistances between vertically aligned blocks on different dies are large, so hot blocks should not be stacked directly on each other.

## Going deeper

Cong, Wei and Zhang, "A thermal-driven floorplanning algorithm for 3D ICs", ICCAD (2004); Huang and others, "HotSpot: a compact thermal modeling methodology", IEEE Transactions on VLSI Systems (2006).

label: Multi-die assembly verification
lesson:
# Multi-die assembly verification

Single-die DRC and LVS prove one die correct against its own netlist. A multi-die package adds new ways to fail: bumps that do not line up between dies, a die flipped or rotated the wrong way, nets connected to the wrong neighbour pin, or package wiring that does not match the system netlist. Multi-die verification extends physical verification to the assembly, using a description of how dies are placed and connected.

## The assembly description

Assembly verification needs a machine-readable description of the stack: which dies are present, their placement, rotation and flip in a common coordinate system, which interfaces connect, and a system-level netlist that says which bump of one die connects to which bump of another or to the package. Without it, a checker sees only separate layouts. Face-to-face bonding mirrors one die, so coordinates must be transformed consistently, and a single transform error shifts every bump. Industry formats and open descriptions for 3D assemblies exist for exactly this reason. The verification engine treats the description as the source of truth, so it must itself be checked against the design intent.

## Interface DRC

Interface DRC checks the geometry where dies meet. Bump or pad centres on both sides must align within tolerance, pad sizes and pitches must match the bonding rules, and keep-out regions such as TSV zones must not collide with active circuits on the other die. It also checks alignment marks, dummy pads for planarity in hybrid bonding, and minimum distances to die edges. Because each die was checked separately against its own rules, the interface checker works on a merged view, often only the top layers and bump layers of each die, transformed into the shared frame. A misalignment of one pitch is a classic error that single-die DRC cannot find.

## Assembly LVS

Assembly LVS proves that the physical connections between dies and the package implement the intended system netlist. It extracts connectivity through each die's bump layer, the interposer or substrate wiring, and the bonds between them, then compares the resulting graph with the system netlist, the same graph-matching idea as die LVS at a coarser level. Typical findings are swapped bump assignments, power nets shorted to ground through a package plane, and an unconnected redundant lane. Since dies can come from different teams or vendors, assembly LVS often uses abstract views of each die, only its bump-level pins, so the IP of each die stays private while the connections are verified.

## Going deeper

Lim, "Design for High Performance, Low Power, and Reliable 3D Integrated Circuits" (2013); the IEEE Heterogeneous Integration Roadmap chapter on co-design and simulation tools.

label: Multiphysics engines in the four-layer model
lesson:
# Multiphysics engines in the four-layer model

Package and 3D-IC analysis runs on multiphysics engines: thermal solvers, mechanical FEA, power-integrity and electromigration checkers, and the coupling between them. An agent that customizes these engines must know which part is immutable core and which is change surface. The four-layer engine model sorts every request into core, policy, parameter or hook, and the change tiers say how each is made and reviewed.

## Core and change surface of a multiphysics engine

In a thermal or mechanical solver the core is the discretization and the numerical kernel: assembling the conductance or stiffness matrix from the mesh, enforcing boundary conditions, and the sparse solver with its convergence test. Energy conservation and the material law are invariants. The change surface is everything that varies by customer and package: material libraries with temperature-dependent properties, mesh-refinement policies, which coupling scheme to use (loose iteration or monolithic Newton), convergence tolerances, the power maps imported from chip tools, and the reports to produce. Hooks expose live state such as per-die peak temperature, the coupling residual and the joint strain, so an agent can watch a run and decide what to do next.

## Placing a request in a tier

Tier 1 is configuration: a new material card, a tighter tolerance, a different heat-transfer coefficient, a new report. No code changes. Tier 2 is a plug-in at a defined seam: a new material model such as a creep law for a new solder, a new power-map importer, or a new boundary-condition type such as a two-phase cold plate, written against the engine's material or boundary interface. Tier 3 is a core edit: changing how the matrix is assembled, or replacing the solver. A request to model a new interface material with a known conductivity is Tier 1; a request to model its pressure-dependent bond line needs a Tier 2 material plug-in. A seam is well placed when such requests never reach Tier 3.

## Seam design for coupled physics

Coupling is where multiphysics engines most need good seams. A clean design exposes a field-exchange interface: each single-physics solver publishes fields such as power density, temperature and displacement on its own mesh, and a coupler maps them between meshes and decides when to iterate. Then a new coupling, for example temperature-dependent electrical resistance feeding back into power, is a coupler policy rather than an edit inside both solvers. The seam must carry enough context: mesh, units, time, and validity ranges of each material. Calls should be coarse, per field and per iteration, not per element, so the kernels stay fast. Everything must be deterministic so that a differential test can compare runs.

## Going deeper

The agent-first EDA concepts in this curriculum's agentic domain; Keyes and others, "Multiphysics simulations: challenges and opportunities", International Journal of High Performance Computing Applications (2013).

label: Fast thermal surrogates versus accurate solvers
prereqs: Fast and accurate engines in a modeling loop
lesson:
# Fast thermal surrogates versus accurate solvers

An agent exploring package and 3D floorplans cannot run a full thermal solve for every candidate. It uses a fast engine, a compact resistance model or a learned surrogate, inside the loop, and recurses to the accurate finite-element or finite-volume solver when the fast answer is not trustworthy. Knowing what the fast engine gives up, and when to recurse, is what keeps the loop both quick and correct.

## What a fast thermal engine trades away

A compact thermal model lumps each block or die into a few nodes and solves a small network in microseconds. A learned surrogate maps a power map and stack description to a temperature map in milliseconds. Both trade resolution and generality for speed. A compact model misses hot spots smaller than its blocks and assumes fixed boundary conditions. A surrogate is accurate only near its training distribution of stacks, materials and power maps. Neither captures nonlinearity well: temperature-dependent conductivity and leakage feedback are often linearized. For ranking candidate floorplans these errors are tolerable when they shift all candidates similarly. For signoff they are not, because the limit is the absolute peak temperature.

## When to recurse to the accurate solver

The agent should call the accurate solver when the fast answer is near a decision boundary, when the input leaves the surrogate's validated range, or when candidates are too close to rank. Concretely: a predicted peak within a margin of the junction limit, a new material or cooling solution not in the training set, a hot block smaller than the compact model's resolution, or two floorplans whose predicted peaks differ by less than the surrogate's error. It should also recurse periodically to measure the surrogate's current error on real candidates. Recursion results become new training or calibration data, so the fast engine improves where the search actually spends its time.

## Measuring surrogate error honestly

A surrogate's error must be measured on held-out designs that resemble the ones the agent will explore, and reported on the quantity that matters, the peak temperature and its location, not an average over all grid points. A small mean error can hide a large error at the hot spot. The error also depends on where the search goes: an optimizer drives toward unusual designs where the surrogate may be wrong in its favour, the classic proxy-exploitation problem. The guard is to verify the final candidates with the accurate solver, track the fast-versus-accurate gap over the run, and refuse to report a surrogate-only result as a signoff temperature.

## Going deeper

Huang and others, "HotSpot: a compact thermal modeling methodology", IEEE Transactions on VLSI Systems (2006); the agentic domain concept on fast and accurate engines.

C) Ranking needs higher accuracy than signoff

D) Fast models are never used for ranking
problems.a: Ranking tolerates errors shared by all candidates; signoff needs the absolute peak
problems.e: A common bias cancels in comparisons but not against an absolute limit.

A learned thermal surrogate is accurate on its test set. Where is it least trustworthy?

A) On designs the accurate solver already checked

B) On stacks, materials or power maps outside its training distribution

C) On designs similar to its training data

D) On designs with lower total power
problems.a: On stacks, materials or power maps outside its training distribution
problems.e: Surrogates interpolate; extrapolation is where they fail silently.

B) Average the two

C) Evaluate both with the accurate solver before choosing

D) Pick the lower one immediately
problems.a: Evaluate both with the accurate solver before choosing
problems.e: A difference smaller than the error cannot rank candidates.

problems.q:
A surrogate predicts a peak of 103 °C against a 105 °C limit with a known error of plus or minus 4 K. What should the agent do?

A) Reject the design outright

B) Recurse to the accurate solver, since the decision is within the surrogate's error

C) Accept the design as passing

D) Retrain the surrogate before anything else
problems.a: Recurse to the accurate solver, since the decision is within the surrogate's error
problems.e: Near a decision boundary, only the accurate engine can decide.

B) Accept the design as passing

C) Reject the design outright

D) Retrain the surrogate before anything else
problems.a: Recurse to the accurate solver, since the decision is within the surrogate's error
problems.e: Near a decision boundary, only the accurate engine can decide.

B) The accurate solver must be wrong

C) The optimizer found a region where the surrogate is wrong in its favour

D) The ambient temperature changed
problems.a: The optimizer found a region where the surrogate is wrong in its favour

label: Chiplet partitioning agents and their rewards
lesson:
# Chiplet partitioning agents and their rewards

A chiplet partitioning agent proposes how to split a system into dies, which process each die uses, and how they connect, then scores the result with tools: cost and yield models, a partitioner for cut size, die-to-die bandwidth and energy models, and thermal checks. Training such an agent with tool-grounded rewards is promising, but the reward must reflect the real objective or the agent will optimize the proxy instead.

## A tool-grounded reward

The reward combines terms that engines compute deterministically: silicon cost per good system from area and yield models, assembly and package cost, the bandwidth and energy of cut nets from interface models, peak temperature from a thermal model, and constraint penalties for exceeding reticle size, bump capacity or shoreline. Each term is grounded: it comes from a tool, not from the agent's own estimate. The terms must be normalized so none dominates by unit choice, and hard constraints should reject a candidate rather than add a small penalty, or the agent will trade a violated constraint for a small gain elsewhere.

## How the reward gets gamed

A reward computed by fast models invites exploitation. An agent may cut a design into many tiny chiplets because the yield model rewards small dies while the interface overhead model underestimates PHY area. It may minimize cut size by putting heavily communicating blocks on one die that exceeds the thermal budget when the thermal term is coarse. It may choose a bump pitch the cost model treats as free. Each is the agent finding where the model is wrong. Defences include accurate-engine audits of top candidates, penalties tied to model confidence, adversarial tests of the reward on known bad partitions, and keeping the scoring tools read-only to the agent.

## Proxy reward against signoff quality

The fast reward is a proxy for what the product needs: a partition that closes timing across dies, meets power-integrity and thermal signoff, and yields at the predicted cost. The gap between proxy and signoff must be measured, by taking a sample of agent proposals through full implementation and comparing their signoff metrics with the proxy scores. If the rank correlation is low, the reward is not teaching the right thing, regardless of how high the proxy scores climb. A useful practice is to track the proxy-to-signoff correlation as a first-class training metric, and to stop or retune training when proxy scores rise while sampled signoff quality does not.

## Going deeper

Feng and Ma, "Chiplet actuary", DAC (2022); the agentic domain concept on tool-grounded reinforcement learning.

problems.e: Proxy improvement without signoff improvement is reward hacking or misalignment.

label: Golden multiphysics checks
lesson:
# Golden multiphysics checks

Before an agent's change to a multiphysics engine or flow is accepted, it must pass golden and differential tests. Golden tests compare the engine with known answers; differential tests compare the changed engine with the baseline on reference designs, proving that only the intended results moved. For thermal, mechanical and electromigration engines, the known answers come from closed-form physics and from measurements.

## Golden cases from closed-form physics

Good golden tests for multiphysics engines have exact answers. For thermal: a 1-D slab with fixed temperatures, whose resistance is $L/(kA)$; a chain with distributed heating, whose far-end rise is $RqN(N+1)/2$; a lumped body's step response $PR(1 - e^{-t/\tau})$. For mechanics: a bilayer strip, whose curvature follows Timoshenko's formula; a constrained thin film, whose stress is $E\Delta\alpha\Delta T/(1-\nu)$. For coupling: a self-heating resistor, whose converged temperature has a closed form and whose runaway current is known. Each should pass to a tolerance tied to mesh resolution, and the suite should include mesh-refinement checks showing the expected convergence order.

## Differential checks on reference designs

A differential test runs baseline and changed engines on reference packages and compares every reported quantity: per-die peak temperatures and their locations, warpage across the temperature profile, joint strains, current densities. A change that should affect only one thing, say a new creep model for one solder, must leave thermal results identical to the last bit and move only the mechanical results of assemblies that use that solder. Any unexpected movement elsewhere is a regression or a hidden coupling. The check needs deterministic engines, seeded meshing and stable ordering, otherwise numerical noise hides real differences.

## Measured ground truth

Closed forms cover simple geometry; measurements anchor real packages. Thermal test dies with embedded heaters and sensors give junction temperatures for known power maps. Shadow moiré gives warpage across the reflow profile. Accelerated cycling gives joint lives. A golden suite should include a few such measured cases with their uncertainty, and the engine passes when its prediction falls within that uncertainty. These cases also detect drift in material libraries, a common silent failure: a changed modulus table can pass every closed-form test and still mispredict a real package. Measurements are design and process data, so they stay inside the IP boundary, with only pass or fail results shared.

## Going deeper

Oberkampf and Roy, "Verification and Validation in Scientific Computing" (2010); the agentic domain concept on golden and differential testing.

problems.q:
What golden case checks a coupled electro-thermal solver?

A) A pure thermal slab

B) A self-heating resistor whose converged temperature and runaway current have closed forms

C) A mechanical bilayer strip

D) A purely electrical resistor network
problems.a: A self-heating resistor whose converged temperature and runaway current have closed forms
problems.e: Only a coupled case with a closed form exercises the coupling.

problems.q:
Besides matching closed forms, what should a golden suite show under mesh refinement?

A) That memory use falls

B) The expected order of convergence toward the exact answer

C) That runtime stays constant

D) That the answer does not change at all
problems.a: The expected order of convergence toward the exact answer
problems.e: Convergence order verifies the discretization is implemented as designed.

problems.q:
What golden case checks a coupled electro-thermal solver?

A) A mechanical bilayer strip

B) A pure thermal slab

C) A purely electrical resistor network

D) A self-heating resistor whose converged temperature and runaway current have closed forms
problems.a: A self-heating resistor whose converged temperature and runaway current have closed forms
problems.e: Only a coupled case with a closed form exercises the coupling.

problems.q:
A differential run shows thermal peaks moved by 0.01 K although only a mechanical model changed. What does it indicate?

A) Proof the change is correct

B) Normal noise to ignore

C) An improvement to the thermal solver

D) A regression, a hidden coupling or nondeterminism that must be explained before acceptance
problems.a: A regression, a hidden coupling or nondeterminism that must be explained before acceptance
problems.e: Unexpected movement in unrelated outputs is exactly what differential testing exists to catch.

problems.q:
Why must meshing be seeded and deterministic for differential tests?

A) Random meshes are less accurate

B) Seeds speed up solving

C) Determinism is only cosmetic

D) Otherwise mesh noise hides or imitates real differences between baseline and change
problems.a: Otherwise mesh noise hides or imitates real differences between baseline and change
problems.e: Comparisons need identical inputs apart from the change itself.

problems.q:
A plug-in adds a creep model for one new solder. What must the differential test show?

A) Only that the run finishes

B) That warpage improves everywhere

C) Thermal results are identical, and mechanical results move only for assemblies using that solder

D) All results move slightly
problems.a: Thermal results are identical, and mechanical results move only for assemblies using that solder
problems.e: Differential checks prove only the intended outputs changed.

problems.q:
When does a measured golden case pass?

A) Whenever the solver converges

B) When the prediction is lower than the measurement

C) When the prediction falls within the measurement's uncertainty

D) When the prediction matches to every digit
problems.a: When the prediction falls within the measurement's uncertainty
problems.e: Measured truth has uncertainty, and the acceptance band must reflect it.

problems.q:
What should happen to an agent's engine change that passes golden tests but fails one differential check?

A) It is promoted with a warning

B) It is promoted, since golden tests passed

C) It is not promoted until the differential failure is explained or fixed

D) The differential baseline is updated to match
problems.a: It is not promoted until the differential failure is explained or fixed
problems.e: Nothing is promoted without passing both kinds of test.

problems.q:
Thermal test-die measurements are customer process data. How do they enter a shared golden suite?

A) They are discarded

B) They stay inside the IP boundary, and only pass or fail results are shared

C) They are pasted into the agent's prompt

D) They are uploaded to a public benchmark
problems.a: They stay inside the IP boundary, and only pass or fail results are shared
problems.e: The IP boundary is part of the architecture; know-how flows out, design data does not.

label: Agentic package co-design loops
lesson:
# Agentic package co-design loops

An agentic package co-design loop reads the reports of package, board, thermal and power-integrity tools, proposes changes such as ball reassignments, decap placement, die order or TIM choice, runs them through the engines and iterates until signoff passes, with a human approving the final change. It is the package-level counterpart of an agentic timing ECO loop, and it needs the same discipline about what it may change and how it proves its changes.

## What the loop reads and proposes

The loop reads structured reports: impedance profiles against the target, IR drop and current per ball and bump, escape-routing completion, per-die temperatures, warpage and joint strain. It maps each violation to candidate fixes from a library: add power balls under a hot region, move decoupling capacitors closer, swap die order in the stack, change the TIM, reassign signals to outer rows. Each proposal is a small, typed edit to the design database, such as a ball-map change or a stackup parameter, not free-form text. Typed edits can be validated before any engine runs, and they make the history of the loop reviewable.

## Seams the loop needs

The loop works only if engines expose seams for its changes. A ball-assignment interface lets it move a net between balls and re-run escape routing incrementally. A material and stackup interface lets it swap a TIM or substrate core without editing the solver. A power-map interface lets the chip team's power model update the thermal run. Through these, most fixes are Tier 1 configuration or Tier 2 plug-ins. A fix that requires editing an engine's core, say a new way to compute plane inductance, is out of scope for the loop and goes to engine developers. Each engine should also support incremental runs, because the loop's speed depends on not redoing the whole analysis after each small edit.

## Convergence and approval

Co-design fixes interact: moving power balls helps IR drop but may block escape routing, and a thicker TIM bond line from warpage undoes a thermal fix. The loop must therefore re-run every affected check after each change, not only the one it targeted, and track a global violation count so it can detect oscillation between two fixes. It should stop when signoff passes, when no proposal improves the count, or when a budget of iterations is spent. The final change goes to a human as a diff of the ball map, stackup and material choices with before-and-after reports. The human approves; the loop never signs off its own work.

## Going deeper

Swaminathan and Engin, "Power Integrity Modeling and Design for Semiconductors and Systems" (2007); the agentic domain concept on signoff and ECO loops.
